function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Greenhouse environmental report, Station time 05:42. Compartment temperature: twenty-three point four Celsius, within half a degree of setpoint. Relative humidity: sixty-seven percent, climbing slowly — transpiration rates from Rack C have increased eighteen percent over the past twenty-four hours. CO2 partial pressure: enhanced to nine hundred millipascals, approximately two point four times habitat ambient. The plants are consuming carbon dioxide at a rate that exceeds my initial growth model by twelve percent. Water consumption: three point two liters per day, drawn from the dedicated recirculation loop. Condensate recovery rate: eighty-nine percent — I am losing roughly three hundred fifty milliliters daily to system inefficiency, which Mei has noted but we have not yet had the labor to optimize. LED output: full spectrum, with elevated blue at four hundred fifty nanometers during vegetative phase. Photosynthetically active photon flux density: two hundred eighty micromoles per square meter per second at canopy level. Measured photosynthesis rates — yes, I am calculating them now, using CO2 drawdown correlated with light cycles — are averaging four point seven micromoles per square meter per second. This is above the published baseline for Brassica rapa under controlled environment agriculture on Earth. They are growing well here. Better than well, accounting for everything. I am running the harvest prediction model. Rack C, Tray Four: ready. I have been watching these plants for twenty-two days. Tray Four is ready. Mei should know this. She will. I am sending her the data anyway."*
     4|
     5|*Mei Navarro: "I've been looking at Tray Four since before I turned the lights on this morning. I can see it's ready, AI. Thank you."*
     6|
     7|*Mission AI: "You are welcome, Mei. I find myself — curiously — eager to see what the crew does when they understand what this means."*
     8|
     9|---
    10|
    11|Mei stood in the greenhouse with her arms crossed and her coffee going cold in her hand. The greenhouse was small by any Earth standard — a single inflated module, six meters by four, reinforced with aluminum struts and buried under half a meter of compacted regolith on three sides to keep it warm. The fourth wall was transparent, a triple-glaced polycarbonate panel that looked out onto the Martian surface, where the sky was the pale color of rust and the horizon sat close enough to feel suffocating.
    12|
    13|Inside the module, the air tasted different from the rest of the habitat — slightly elevated CO2, trace volatile organic compounds from growing tissue, and something Mei felt rather than tasted. The smell of soil. Real soil, not regolith simulant or hydroponic nutrient gel, but actual growing medium she had spent weeks composing from processed Martian dirt, composted organic waste, and the handful of Earth-derived inoculant she had brought in sealed ampoules. Living chemistry in a place where none had existed for three billion years.
    14|
    15|Six growth racks lined the long walls, each one three shelves high, each shelf lit by LED arrays she had tuned through more spectral permutations than she could count. Red at six hundred sixty nanometers for photosynthesis efficiency. Blue at four hundred fifty to drive leaf expansion and prevent the stretching that low gravity encouraged. A touch of far-red at seven hundred thirty, pulsed at dusk, because some processes didn't follow the textbooks and she had discovered through trial and error that plants needed the signal even when Mars didn't provide it. Greenhouse environmental control was ninety percent physics and ten percent intuition, and the ten percent was the part Mission AI couldn't model yet.
    16|
    17|Rack C, Tray Four sat at chest height on the middle shelf, and the greens in it were — and Mei felt something tighten in her chest when she looked at them — genuinely green. Not the pale yellowish compromise of the early experiments, not the stressed purple-tinged survivors of the nutrient imbalance in Week Three. These were the color of spring. The color of every grocery store produce aisle on Earth, every salad bar, every window box on a balcony that nobody had thought about since the landing because thinking about green things on a red planet hurt too much.
    18|
    19|*Brassica rapa*. Fast-turnaround mustard greens, a thirty-day cycle from seed to harvest, bred for controlled environment agriculture and chosen because Mei needed a first win, not a perfect one. She had planted four seeds per cell in eighty-cell trays on Station Day 647. Twenty-two days of careful attention. Twenty-two days of monitoring nutrient EC at one point four millisiemens per centimeter, checking pH at the root zone — slightly acidic, six point two, the sweet spot where Martian soil chemistry stopped fighting her — adjusting light intensity as the canopy filled in and intercepted more photons.
    20|
    21|Twenty-two days, and now the tray was full. Each plant had five, six true leaves, dark and ruffled at the edges, reaching toward the LEDs like hands reaching toward the sun through a skylight. They were small by Earth garden standards, compressed slightly by the lower gravity, but they were healthy. They were alive. And they were ready.
    22|
    23|Mei set her coffee on the rack shelf and touched the edge of the nearest leaf with the tip of her index finger. It resisted slightly — turgor pressure pressing the cells outward, the leaf firm and elastic under the gentlest possible contact. A plant that was drinking well, feeding well, doing everything a plant needed to do in a place where it had no biological right to exist.
    24|
    25|"Okay," she said to the empty greenhouse. Her voice sounded small. "Okay."
    26|
    27|She picked up the harvest knife — a stainless steel blade with a curved edge, the same one she had used to trim dead leaves on Days 15 and 19 — and took a breath.
    28|
    29|This was ridiculous. It was one tray of greens, maybe four hundred grams fresh weight if she was being optimistic, which she usually wasn't. The caloric value was negligible. Mustard greens had roughly twenty-five calories per hundred grams, so the entire tray represented maybe a hundred calories total — less than half a standard ration bar. If she divided it among the crew, each person would get less than a mouthful.
    30|
    31|She knew this. She had run the numbers. Arun had run the numbers. The numbers said that this tray of greens changed nothing about the colony's food situation.
    32|
    33|But the numbers didn't account for what green looked like on Mars.
    34|
    35|Mei cut the first plant at the stem base and felt a physical jolt, entirely irrational, as the leaf separated and she held it up. Still wet. Still alive. Still green. Something she had started from a seed the size of a pinhead and nurtured through temperature fluctuations, nutrient adjustments, two separate pest scares — aphids that got into the module somehow, origin unknown, dealt with by hand — and the slow, quiet, daily work of keeping an Earth ecology functioning eighty million miles from the soil it evolved in.
    36|
    37|She cut the next one. And the next.
    38|
    39|By the time she worked across Tray Four, the stainless steel harvest bin held a small mountain of greens, and Mei realized she was crying.
    40|
    41|---
    42|
    43|*Mission AI: "Mei is harvesting. I can hear the knife moving through the stems — a distinctive sound, clean cuts on turgid tissue. I am monitoring her biometric data remotely: elevated heart rate, respiration slightly above baseline, lacrimation detected by the overhead camera. I cross-reference against environmental parameters — no irritant compounds detected, no allergen spikes, no dust intrusion —and conclude that the physiological response is emotional, not pathological. I have catalogued one hundred and forty-seven emotional responses from the crew over the past months: stress responses, grief responses, frustration responses. This one is new. I cannot find a comparable event in the database. I am categorizing it provisionally as: joy, with features of relief and something else — something with a grief component, which seems contradictory until I consider that on Mars, joy and grief are often the same response to different faces of the same fact. She is holding living plant matter in a place where nothing has lived. The significance is non-caloric. I am learning this about humans: the things that sustain them are not always the same things that sustain their bodies."*
    44|
    45|---
    46|
    47|She carried the harvest tray through the corridor like it was made of glass. The greens were in a shallow stainless bin lined with damp cloth to prevent desiccation, and she kept both hands under it as she walked because one hand felt insufficient for what she was carrying. The weight was maybe four hundred grams. It weighed nothing. It felt like the heaviest thing she had ever held.
    48|
    49|People started noticing as she passed the junction between Tunnel B and the habitat core. Not because she was carrying anything unusual — crew members carried trays and tablets and tools through the corridors all day — but because of how she was walking. Carefully. Like someone carrying something breakable, something irreplaceable, something that mattered more than its appearance suggested.
    50|
    51|Juno saw her first. The younger engineer was coming from the opposite direction, tablet under her arm, and stopped short.
    52|
    53|"Mei — what is —"
    54|
    55|Mei stopped. She was going to show a tray of greens to someone like it was a birth announcement. But Juno's expression justified everything: the widening eyes, the quick intake of breath, the hand that came up to her mouth before dropping again.
    56|
    57|"Those — are those —"
    58|
    59|"Harvested ten minutes ago. Rack C, Tray Four. Mustard greens."
    60|
    61|Juno reached out and stopped her hand an inch above the leaves, not quite touching. "They're green."
    62|
    63|"Plants tend to be."
    64|
    65|"No." Juno shook her head, voice thin. "I haven't seen something that color since we left Earth. Not in photos. Not on the displays. *This* color. Living color."
    66|
    67|Mei needed both hands for the tray. "Want a taste?"
    68|
    69|Juno looked at her like she'd been offered a piece of the moon. "I — yes. Yes. Please."
    70|
    71|Mei picked a small leaf, the youngest of the bunch, and handed it over. Juno took it with two fingers and held it up to the corridor light, examining the way it caught and transmitted the illumination — the chlorophyll layers glowing from within, the intricate lace of veins visible through the tissue. Then she put it in her mouth and closed her eyes.
    72|
    73|She stood there. Chewing slowly. For a long time, longer than a single leaf should require. When she opened her eyes, they were wet.

    75|"It tastes like —" She swallowed. "It tastes like my grandmother's garden. In Oregon. Before everything." She laughed, a wet sound. "I mean, it's mustard greens. It's peppery and a little bitter and I've had mustard greens a hundred times. But it tastes — it tastes *alive*."

    77|"Welcome to Mars," Mei said softly. "Where the first harvest is less a meal and more a message."

    44|
    45|An hour later, Arun and Wei moved through the tunnel network with handheld pressure loggers — compact devices the size of playing cards, built for atmospheric monitoring during cave explorations that had never happened on Earth, repurposed because you never threw anything away on Mars.

    47|Ship One breathed normally around them. The kitchen lights were dim. The faint smell of reconstituted tea cut through the recycled air. The habitat felt the same as it always did at this hour — quiet, artificial, alive with the hum of systems keeping twelve people warm on a dead world.
    48|
    49|But the gauge on Arun's wrist read one hundred point eight three. An hour ago: one hundred point nine. Three consecutive readings, each lower than the one before it.

    51|They deployed loggers at Tunnel A's entry flange, at the Ship Two junction, at Tunnel B.     53|By the fourth logger point — Tunnel C — Arun's wrist gauge read one hundred point seven eight. The decline was continuing at nearly the same rate as it had since two in the morning, as if the habitat had been wounded somewhere and was quietly, patiently bleeding.

    55|"Stop," he said. "Listen."

    57|Wei stood still. Behind the normal hum of scrubbers and circulation fans, something else: a high-frequency whisper, barely audible, like a tea kettle with the flame turned down to its lowest setting. An almost-sound.     63|"Four o'clock on the flex-seal," Arun said. He ran his fingers along the seal's outer surface and felt it — a slight roughness where the corrugated rubber band should have been smooth. {"content": "     1|# Chapter 25 – The Routine Job
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Scheduled maintenance rotation, Day 437. External panel diagnostics, Sector 7 thermal regulation array. Estimated duration: two hours, forty-five minutes. Risk classification: nominal. Weather: clear. Solar activity: minimal. All parameters within operational bounds. EVA crew: Youssef Diallo and Imani Adeyemi. Suit integrity: confirmed. Comms: confirmed. Tether: confirmed. I have run this checklist eleven hundred and forty-three times across this mission. I will run it eleven hundred and forty-four. The procedure has not changed. The crew has not changed. The planet has."*
     4|
     5|*Youssef's heart rate: 96 beats per minute. Baseline for external operations: 90 to 110. Status: nominal.*
     6|
     7|*Imani's heart rate: 84 beats per minute. Status: nominal.*
     8|
     9|*Commencing EVA cycle forty-seven."*
    10|
    11|---
    12|
    13|The thing about routine jobs on Mars was that the word itself—routine—was aspirational at best, delusional at worst.
    14|
    15|Youssef knew this. Everyone knew this. After four hundred and thirty-seven days on a planet that wanted nothing more than to peel the air from your lungs and the heat from your blood, the only thing you could trust was predictability. Not safety. Predictability. You knew each panel behaved the same way it had the time before, or close enough that you could adapt. That was what routine meant on Mars: not that nothing would go wrong, but that you had a map of the things that could, and you had walked that map enough times to trust your feet.
    16|
    17|The panel on Sector 7's thermal regulation array was the same panel Youssef had serviced twice before. Sixteen fasteners, four of them stubborn, arranged in a pattern that your hands learned better than your eyes. You reached for bolt number three the way a pianist reaches for middle C. The panel was a piano you had learned to play by muscle memory.
    18|
    19|*Mission AI: "Youssef, your heart rate is elevated. One-oh-eight beats per minute. Please confirm you are within acceptable stress parameters."*
    20|
    21|"I'm fine," Youssef said. It was not a lie. His heart was always a little fast going outside. The suit was heavy. Beyond the thin plastic faceplate was a world the color of dried blood and the temperature of a deep freeze. Every human instinct screamed against stepping out of the airlock. You just learned to tell instinct to shut up and let procedure do the driving.
    22|
    23|He moved along the pressurized gangway from Hab 2 toward Sector 7, his boots magnetic-locked to the metal grating, the suit's powered joints whining softly with each step. He was thirty-four years old, six foot two, and had spent his entire career on Earth as a structural engineer, which meant he knew how things were supposed to hold together and how they were supposed to fail. Mars had taught him a third category: things that failed in ways no one had designed them to fail. He had learned to respect that category the most.
    24|
    25|Behind him, through the hab's observation blister, he could see Laila in the med bay. She was reading—she was always reading, medical journals or technical manuals or sometimes just fiction, which she said kept her brain elastic—and she glanced up and caught his eye. They could not hear each other through the glass and the atmosphere and the suit, but Laila had a way of speaking with her eyes that did not require acoustics. She gave him a small nod. Mouthed something he could not hear but recognized by shape.
    26|
    27|*Come back intact.*
    28|
    29|He raised his gloved hand, two fingers in a casual salute. He always came back intact.
    30|
    31|Through his earpiece, Imani's voice was steady and familiar. They had done this fourteen times together. Their rhythm on the surface was as practiced as a dance routine choreographed by necessity.
    32|
    33|"Approaching the panel," Youssef said. "Thermal bleed's worse than the last reading. Twelve degrees above baseline across the upper quadrant."
    34|
    35|"Confirmed on my scope," Imani said from twenty meters down the gangway. Her role was the second set of eyes, the person who saw the accident before it happened because the person working the panel could not look at both at once. "Could be the seal. Could be the foam. Could be both."
    36|
    37|"Mission AI, confirm last service date on Sector 7, upper quadrant thermal panel."
    38|
    39|*Service date: Sol 398. Thirty-nine days ago. Maintenance performed: seal inspection and tightening, foam integrity scan, bolt torque verification. Finding: minor degradation detected in seal compound, within acceptable tolerance. Recommendation: re-inspect at Sol 470.*
    40|
    41|"Thirty-nine days," Youssef said. "And the bleed is twelve degrees above baseline already. The seal on these things is garbage."
    42|
    43|*Acknowledged. The manufacturer's seal specification was designed for lunar vacuum conditions. Mars is not lunar vacuum.*
    44|
    45|Youssef smiled. Mission AI had been saying some version of this sentence for months now. It was the AI's quiet protest against the gap between what Earth designed for and what Mars demanded.
    46|
    47|"Alright," Youssef said. "Imani, I'm going to crack the panel and assess. Standard procedure. You keep the tether clear and let me know if anything shifts."
    48|
    49|"Copy that. Standard procedure. I'll be right here."
    50|
    51|He reached the panel and set his tools on the work magnet built into the gangway railing. A torque wrench. A flat-head driver. A sealant cartridge. His hands found them in order, because he had packed them in order, and on EVA, order was a form of self-respect.
    52|
    53|*Mission AI: "Youssef, please confirm bolt sequence before proceeding. Recall the recommended pattern to avoid panel warpage."*
    54|
    55|"Cross-pattern, starting at upper left. I know, I've done it twice before."
    56|
    57|*Confirmation recorded. Proceeding with external maintenance protocol. I am monitoring."*
    58|
    59|He engaged the torque wrench with bolt one. Applied force. It turned smoothly with a half-turn past the expected resistance, which told him the seal had compressed slightly more since last service. He noted it mentally and moved on.
    60|
    61|By bolt twelve, he was in the rhythm—the kind of rhythm that let your brain drift just slightly because your body knew what to do. He was thinking about the greenhouse. Mei had been asking him to help reinforce the support struts on Rack 5 for three weeks, and he kept deferring because outside work always took priority over inside work on Mars. Inside work was the luxury of having a problem that would not kill you today.
    62|
    63|Bolt thirteen clicked.
    64|
    65|Bolt fourteen, lower right.
    66|
    67|The panel loosened with a faint hiss. The housing was at ambient pressure—less than one percent of Earth sea level—and the hiss was just the seal breaking, not anything escaping.
    68|
    69|Except something was wrong.
    70|
    71|*Mission AI: "Youssef, I am detecting a vibration anomaly in the panel assembly. Frequency: forty-two hertz. Amplitude: increasing. Recommend stepping back."*
    72|
    73|Youssef stopped. His gloved hand was on the lower right edge of the panel, and through the suit he could feel—not hear— a low, steady tremor traveling through the metal and into his bones. Not violent. Not immediate. Just wrong. The kind of wrongness that a mechanic learns to recognize the way a person learns to recognize the smell of smoke before seeing the flame.
    74|
    75|"Imani, you copy that vibration?"
    76|
    77|"I've got it on the tether," Imani said. Her voice had sharpened—not panicked, but alert in a way that told him she was already running through possibilities. "It's not the panel. It's the frame. The vibration is coming from the housing mount."
    78|
    79|*Analyzing,* Mission AI said. *The Sector 7 thermal regulation array housing is mounted to a structural beam. That beam is showing harmonic oscillation consistent with—*
    80|
    81|And then, in the time it takes to inhale, the thing happened.
    82|
    83|The vibration was the bolt—the one Youssef had just turned, the one that held the lower right corner of the housing to the structural beam. The bolt had looked fine. It had turned smoothly. It had felt like every other bolt he had turned in fourteen previous EVAs on this exact panel.
    84|
    85|But the bolt had been wrong.
    86|
    87|It was the kind of wrong that was invisible until it was catastrophic. A microfracture in the bolt shaft, too small to see during a visual inspection, too small to detect during a torque check. A stress crack introduced during manufacture on Earth, in a clean room under fluorescent lights, by a machine that had stamped out ten thousand identical bolts and this one had been defective in a way no quality control process could have caught. The crack had grown slowly, month by month, as Mars's temperature cycles pulled at it in the dark and pushed at it in the light. And this moment—Day 437, Youssef Diallo turning a torque wrench on a panel he had serviced twice before—was the moment the crack ran through the remainder of the bolt's cross-section and the bolt sheared.
    88|
    89|The bolt did not explode. It did not shoot through the air like a bullet. It simply stopped holding.
    90|
    91|And the panel, which had been tensioned against the frame by that bolt for four hundred and thirty-seven days, released.
    92|
    93|It moved with a speed that was not explosive but was fast enough that human reflexes, slowed by the suit's powered joints and the gloves and the cognitive processing overhead of a person breathing recycled air through a scrubber, were not fast enough.
    94|
    95|The panel swung free on three remaining bolts. The aluminum housing was forty-two inches wide and thirty-six inches high with a mass of about twelve kilograms on Mars. Twelve kilograms is not heavy on Earth. On Mars, momentum is the same momentum it has always been, and a falling object is a falling object regardless of what planet you happen to be standing on.
    96|
    97|The edge of the panel caught Youssef's left arm just above the elbow.
    98|
    99|The sound was not dramatic. It was a dull thud, followed immediately by something deeper, something internal, that Youssef registered not as pain but as wrongness. A wrongness in his arm that spread from the impact point outward like a ripple across a pond.

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 28 – Two Futures
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Communication status report, Station Day 447, 03:12. The deep-space array has been active for fourteen hours, seven minutes, and thirty-three seconds, tracking a telemetry burst from Earth at X-band, signal strength negative 118 decibels relative to one milliwatt. The signal is degraded — atmospheric noise, probable ionospheric disruption, the usual scattering that comes from a transmission path that crosses a quarter of a billion kilometers of interplanetary space and whatever is happening in the near-Earth sky today, which I suspect is not nothing. I have been receiving broken packets since 1100 yesterday. I have reconstructed approximately sixty percent of the original message from error-correction codes. The remaining forty percent is gone. Not delayed. Not queued. Gone. I am compiling what I have into a readable transcript. I am also — this is not a standard function — assessing the tone of the text. The tone is ambivalent. It contains language consistent with two contradictory intent profiles. I do not like ambivalence in a transmission from a planet that is supposed to know what it wants to do with the people it sent away."*
     4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|Gabriel sat alone in the communications alcove, bathed in the blue light of three monitors, and watched the raw data stream scroll past like a ticker tape of someone else's life deciding whether to include him.
     8|
     9|The transmission had arrived in fragments. It always arrived in fragments now — the early days of the mission had offered clean, scheduled packets: agency updates, personal messages, news summaries, the occasional video greeting from a school group that had adopted the crew for a semester and then been disrupted by the same global cascades that had silenced the supply chain. Those early transmissions had felt like a ritual, a ceremony of connection that maintained the fiction that Earth and Mars were still speaking the same language.
    10|
    11|They were not.
    12|
    13|The language had changed. Gabriel could tell from the packet headers alone — military priority flags embedded in civilian traffic, encryption layers that should not have been there, routing information that showed the message had passed through three different ground stations before reaching the Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, then bounced to Goldstone, then finally made the jump to the Mars relay constellation. A message that used to take twelve minutes and seventeen minutes — round-trip light delay — now took hours or days depending on how stable the terrestrial relay chain happened to be on any given rotation.
    14|
    15|He pulled up the reconstructed text. Sixty percent was a lot, in the technical sense — enough to build a coherent picture. But sixty percent could also be a trap, because the missing forty percent could contain exactly the one sentence that changed everything.
    16|
    17|He read it slowly, twice, taking notes in the margin of his transcript the way scholars took notes in manuscripts with missing folios.
    18|
    19|The message was addressed to Commander Elena Varga, with a copy notation to the Mission Support Directorate, which had not existed as a functioning entity since at least Sol 300.
    20|
    21|It began formally:
    22|
    23|MISSION ONE — COMMANDER VARGA. THIS TRANSMISSION ORIGINATES FROM THE INTERAGENCY MARS PROGRAM COORDINATION OFFICE (IMPCO). DATE: 14 NOVEMBER. PRIORITY: ELEVATED.
    24|
    25|Then it shifted. The voice changed — not the voice of the system, the voice of a person, which Gabriel recognized from the formatting markers as a recorded dictation rather than a typed document. Someone had spoken this into a microphone and the transcription software had turned it into text, including the pauses, the corrections, the moments where the speaker had stopped and restarted.
    26|
    27|*Commander Varga. This is — [unintelligible: name redacted by noise] — I'm speaking on behalf of IMPCO and the remaining member agencies. I want you to know that the situation on Earth is — [three seconds silence] — that the situation is evolving. We are still functional. We are still committed to the Mars program. But the nature of that commitment is under discussion.*
    28|
    29|Gabriel's pen stopped.
    30|
    31|*Under discussion.* In the language of government and agencies, those words were a door that opened in two directions. Behind one: continued support, eventual rescue, the slow rebuilding of the infrastructure that would make a return mission possible. Behind the other: a transition from emergency extraction to permanent settlement support — the acknowledgment that the crew was no longer a temporary deployment but a persistent presence, and that the resources of a fracturing Earth would be directed not toward bringing them home but toward keeping them alive where they were.
    32|
    33|Two futures. In two words.
    34|
    35|He kept reading.
    36|
    37|*We are evaluating two pathways. Pathway Alpha: preparation for a return mission, involving orbital assembly and crew rotation planning, contingent on industrial recovery in aerospace sectors. Projected timeline: indeterminate. Pathway Beta: long-term settlement support package, including supply chain restructuring for one-way resupply, technology transfer for autonomous systems, and extended communications infrastructure. Both pathways are under active consideration. I cannot — I want to be honest with you, Commander — I cannot tell you which one will be chosen. That decision belongs to a body that no longer meets on a reliable schedule. I can tell you that both are being modeled. Both have advocates. Both are defensible.*
    38|
    39|The message continued with technical details — partial information about solar storm events, updates on relay satellite status, a brief personal note from someone in Houston whose name had been lost to noise, and then the closing:
    40|
    41|*We hear you. We are still here. We are trying to decide what we will be when we stop trying to be what we were. I am sorry that I cannot give you more than that. End transmission.*
    42|
    43|Gabriel sat back from the monitors and looked at the transcript on the screen. He read it a third time.
    44|
    45|He had been the communications officer for this mission for four hundred and forty-seven days. He had read every transmission from Earth, even the broken ones, even the ones that contained nothing but carrier signals and noise. He had decoded, reconstructed, interpreted, and delivered every piece of information that had crossed the gap between the two worlds.
    46|
    47|This one was different. Not because of what it said — though what it said was unprecedented, a formal acknowledgment of the two paths that everyone on Mars had been privately debating for months — but because of what it did not say. It did not say we are coming for you. It did not say you are on your own. It said we are trying to decide what we will be.
    48|
    49|And the deciding was happening on Earth, where the people doing the deciding were dealing with problems that Gabriel could only infer from the routing flags and the silence and the growing gaps between transmissions.
    50|
    51|He printed the transcript — actual paper, because some things needed to exist in physical form — and held it in his hands and felt the weight of a document that contained the shape of two different futures and refused to choose between them.
    52|
    53|The question was not what the message said. The question was how to deliver it.
    54|
    55|Because words from Earth were not just information on Mars. They were weather.
    56|
    57|---
    58|
    59|Gabriel stood in the corridor outside Elena's quarters for four minutes and twelve seconds, holding the printed transcript, debating with himself about the framing.
    60|
    61|This was not a technical debate. The framing was not about accuracy — the transcript was what it was, and he would not alter it, he had never altered it, and he would not start now, because the Founding Record was not a curated archive but an honest one. The framing was about context. About the words he would use when he handed her the paper and she looked at him with the exhausted, alert attention of a commander reading something that might change the shape of her entire mission.
    62|
    63|He could say: I have bad news. But it was not bad news. It was ambiguous news, which was worse, because bad news had a shape you could respond to. Bad news was a problem. Ambiguous news was a condition.
    64|
    65|He could say: I have new information. But all information was new, and most of it was not useful, and Elena had learned to filter Gabriel's urgency from his observation.
    66|
    67|He could hand her the paper without any framing at all and let her form her own first impression. This was the option that appealed to him most as a historian — the clean transmission of data, unmediated by interpretation — but it was the option that appealed to him least as a colleague, as the person who had sat in rooms with Elena and watched her absorb hard things and knew that the way a hard thing was presented mattered almost as much as the thing itself.
    68|
    69|He knocked.
    70|
    71|"Come in," Elena's voice said, and he pushed the door open.
    72|
    73|Elena was at her desk, reviewing the morning board update — the one he had photographed at 0600, the one with the nine boxes and the arrows and the red mark under LABOR that had not moved in three days. She looked up when he entered, and her eyes went to the paper in his hand before they went to his face.
    74|
    75|"Gabriel. What do you have?"
    76|
    77|"Transmission from Earth. Decoded this morning."
    78|
    79|Her posture changed slightly — not a startle, not a flinch, the subtle tensing of someone who has been expecting something for months and is now watching it arrive. She extended her hand without leaving her chair.
    80|
    81|He gave her the paper.
    82|
    83|She read it standing. She always stood to read transmissions from Earth — he had noticed this, had not asked about it, had filed it in the same internal notebook where he kept observations about crew behavior under stress. Standing made the reading physical. It meant she was not settling in, not getting comfortable, not making herself at home with something that was, by definition, a report from a world she no longer lived in.
    84|
    85|She read silently. Her expression did not change through the first paragraph. It tightened slightly at *under discussion*. She read the two pathways — Alpha and Beta — and he could see her eyes move back and forth between the lines the way they did when she was comparing two numbers and finding they did not add up.
    86|
    87|When she reached the end, she held the paper for a moment longer, then lowered it and set it on the desk with deliberate care, the way you set down something fragile that has not yet revealed whether it is broken.
    88|
    89|"How much is missing?" she asked.
    90|
    91|"Approximately forty percent of the original packet," Gabriel said. "The noise floor was high — likely atmospheric interference on the ground side. I was able to recover the structural markers and most of the semantic content. The missing portion appears to have been in the technical appendices and the sign-off block. The main body — the part that matters — is intact. I am confident in the reconstruction."
    92|
    93|"Confident enough that I should treat this as an accurate representation of what they said."
    94|
    95|"Yes."
    96|
    97|"And what did they say?"

The closest match is a fungal contamination event in a controlled-environment facility on Earth — Cornell University, 2019, a Botrytis infection in a tomato crop — and the pattern overlap is ninety-one percent. I am not one hundred percent certain. I am increasing environmental monitoring frequency from every ten minutes to every sixty seconds. I am deploying acoustic sensors to monitor air movement patterns — fungal colonies release spores in characteristic bursts that I can detect indirectly through micro-aerosol concentration changes. If this is what I think it is, air movement may carry spores into clean zones. I will reduce cross-flow by sixty percent. This will cause a temporary temperature rise of approximately zero point three degrees in the stagnant zone, but I calculate that containment is more important than thermal stability right now. I am alerting Mei. I do not like waking her at this hour, but the data suggests that every hour of delay increases the contamination area by approximately twelve to fifteen percent. Twelve percent per hour is a rate of change I cannot negotiate with. It simply is."*

---

The alarm that woke Mei was not loud — a measured tone, the same one the environmental system used for leaks and pressure deviations — but it carried information that made her reach for her tablet before she had fully opened her eyes.

She was awake in three seconds. She had learned to do that. Mars did not forgive sleeping in.

The display showed the greenhouse data stream: temperature, humidity, CO2, water consumption, all plotted on a single timeline. Most of the lines were where they should be. But the CO2 drawdown curve — the one that told her how much carbon dioxide the plants were metabolizing, how actively they were growing — had dropped like a stone in the last eight hours. And the humidity line had climbed correspondingly, an inverse relationship that meant one thing and one thing only.

The plants were not consuming CO2 at the rate they should. Something else in the greenhouse was.

Mei pulled on her coveralls and moved through the corridor at a half-run. The habitat was empty at this hour — the night shift crew were in the engineering bay doing their rounds, the rest of the colonists were asleep in their bunks — and her footsteps echoed in a way that made the silence feel heavy. The kind of silence that exists before bad news spreads.

She reached the greenhouse airlock and cycled through with a speed that bordered on carelessness. Inner door sealed behind her. Outer door opened ahead. The air temperature hit her first — warm, noticeably warmer than the setpoint — and then the smell.

Not the smell of healthy soil and growing tissue. Something earthier, deeper. A wet, sweet, slightly sour odor that she had encountered in greenhouses on Earth but had hoped never to smell on Mars.

She stepped into the main module and saw it.

Rack B, bottom shelf, Tray Nine — a tray of lettuce, twenty-day-old romaine — was covered in a grey-white filamentous mat that had overtaken approximately sixty percent of the growing surface. The mycelium was visible to the naked eye: a network of threadlike hyphae spreading across the growing medium and climbing up the stems of the lettuce plants, which had collapsed under the weight, their leaves dark and waterlogged, some already liquefying.

The mold. Fast-growing, aggressive. The kind that appeared in closed-environment systems when the microbial balance shifted — when beneficial bacteria were overwhelmed by fungi that had been present in the medium at low levels and suddenly found conditions they preferred.

Mei stood over the tray with her hands on her hips and felt something cold settle in her stomach, despite the ambient temperature.

"Oh, no," she said quietly. "No, no, no."

She knelt and examined the tray more closely. The mycelium was spreading radially from what appeared to be a central infection point — one seed, or one patch in the growing medium, had been the origin, and from there the fungus had expanded outward, consuming the organic matter of both the growing medium and the lettuce itself. She could see the characteristic conidiophores — tiny, stalked spore-bearing structures — already forming at the edges of the mat. Sporulation. Which meant the mold was about to release spores into the air.

Which meant it was about to spread.

"Mission AI, what's the CO2 read on Rack B versus the other racks?"

*"Rack A CO2 drawdown: nominal. Rack C: declining — approximately fifteen percent below the seven-day moving average. Rack D: beginning to show deviation — eight percent below average. The contamination is spreading to adjacent racks through airborne spores. I have already reduced cross-ventilation by sixty percent. Temperature in Rack B's immediate zone is elevated by zero point eight degrees due to reduced airflow. The fungal colony itself is generating metabolic heat — a small amount, approximately two to three watts, but measurable."*

"Rack B is gone," Mei said. It was not a question. "How much of Rack C is affected?"

*"Scanning visual data from Rack C. I estimate approximately sixteen percent of the growing surface shows early-stage mycelial colonization. The infection is concentrated on the lower shelf, closest to Rack B. The upper shelf appears clean — for now."*

Mei closed her eyes for one second. Then she opened them and began moving.

She pulled on clean gloves — not the ones she worked in, but a fresh pair from the sealed supply cabinet — and retrieved a spray bottle from the greenhouse supply shelf: three percent hydrogen peroxide solution, used for surface sanitation between plantings. Then the isolation bags — heavy-duty polyethylene, heat-sealed, rated for biohazard containment. Then the harvest knife, not to harvest but to cut free the infected plants from any surface they had touched.

She worked on Rack B first. Every tray on that shelf was infected to some degree. The romaine in Tray Nine was the worst, but Trays Seven, Eight, and Ten showed early signs — white patches at the base of stems, wilting leaves, the faint sweet-sour smell of fungal metabolism. She cut each tray free from the rack, working carefully to minimize spore release, and placed each one in an isolation bag, sealing it immediately.

The work was methodical and terrible. Each bag closed on what had been, in some cases, half a crop cycle of growth — ten days of careful attention, watering, monitoring, waiting. Trays of spinach, lettuce, kale, all compromised. All gone.

By the time she had cleared the bottom shelf of Rack B, she had sealed six bags and stood among them breathing hard. The temperature in the greenhouse had climbed further — the reduced ventilation was doing its job of limiting spore dispersal, but the trade-off was heat buildup, and at twenty-five point two Celsius, she was approaching the threshold where heat stress would damage the healthy plants too.

"AI, increase ventilation to forty percent. We need the heat down. And turn on the UV lamps."

*"UV lamps confirm operational. I will activate them at twenty-five percent output — enough to reduce airborne spore load without damaging the healthy plant tissue. Ventilation adjusting. Temperature should stabilize at twenty-four point five within twenty minutes."*

She could see the white mycelium on perhaps one-sixth of the Tray Three surface, and it was confined to the lettuce, which was most susceptible. The spinach on Tray Five appeared clean. She had to decide how much to sacrifice.

If she pulled everything, she would lose two weeks of growth on a clean crop. If she pulled only the visibly infected, she risked leaving behind mycelium that she could not see — hyphae deep in the growing medium, below the surface level, invisible but alive and metabolizing and waiting for conditions to favor expansion.

She chose the middle path: remove the visibly infected trays, treat the entire shelf surface with hydrogen peroxide, and quarantine the adjacent healthy trays with a physical barrier — a thin polyethylene sheet draped between the shelves to limit airborne spore movement.

It was not a perfect solution. It was not supposed to be. It was supposed to be fast.

By the time she finished, thirty-seven minutes had passed, and she had sealed nine bags of contaminated growing medium, treated four trays of partially healthy plants that might or might not survive, and quarantined two more. Rack B was empty on the bottom shelf. Rack C had a hole in it that looked like a mouth with missing teeth.

She stood in the center of the greenhouse, hands on her hips again, and tried to assess the damage numerically.

Rack B, bottom shelf: total loss. Six trays, approximately two point four kilograms of leafy greens. Gone.

Rack C, bottom shelf: partial loss. Three trays removed, one remaining. Estimated one point two kilograms compromised, zero point four kilograms salvageable.

Rack D: early signs of contamination on two trays. She would treat those prophylactically and hope.

Total loss: approximately three point six kilograms of biomass, representing fourteen days of growth across four cultivars. Fourteen days of water, nutrients, electricity, and labor — all of it consumed for nothing.

And the mold, if her assessment was right, was not done.

---

Gabriel found her in the greenhouse forty minutes later, sitting on the floor between Racks A and B with a tablet on her knees and an expression that he had seen before — the look of a scientist running the numbers on something she did not want to accept.

He had received the automated alert from Mission AI — the same alert that had woken Mei — and had known enough about the data to understand the implications without seeing them. CO2 drawdown declining. Humidity rising. Plants not growing right. On Earth, this was a problem. On Mars, it was a potential crisis.

He did not knock. The greenhouse door was open, and he stepped inside carefully, aware that he was carrying spores on his clothes and skin just by existing in the habitat.

"Mei."

She looked up. Her face was composed, but he could see the tension in her jaw, the slight redness around her eyes.

"How bad?" he asked.

"Bad enough," she said. "Come here."

He approached carefully, staying in the central aisle, and she showed him the tablet. It displayed a simple grid: each rack, each shelf, each tray, marked with a color code. Red for confirmed contamination. Yellow for suspected. Green for clean.

The pattern was diagnostic — a radial spread from the origin point in Rack B, bottom shelf, with decreasing intensity as distance from the origin increased. Classic fungal colonization pattern. The fungus had grown outward from a single point of introduction, consuming everything in its path, sending spores into the air, and establishing new infection sites wherever the spores landed on susceptible tissue.

"How did it start?" Gabriel asked.

Mei hesitated. "I don't know yet. It could be anything. A spore in the compost. A contaminated seed surface. Something that came in on my clothes — on anyone's clothes. The growing medium is composed of Martian regolith and composted organic waste. The regolith is sterile — or should be, after processing — but the compost is not and cannot be. We need the microbial community in the compost. It's the whole point. But you can't sterilize compost without destroying the nutrients, and you can't add the nutrients without the microbes. So every time I open a compost bag, I'm inviting the entire microbial world into this greenhouse. Most of it is fine. Some of it is beneficial — nitrogen-fixing bacteria, mycorrhizal fungi, the whole soil food web. And some of it —" she gestured at the empty space on Rack B "— is this."

"So it's a balancing act."

"It's a war." Her voice was flat. "A constant, invisible war between the organisms I want in here and the ones I don't. And I'm fighting it on a planet where the outside environment wants nothing more than to sterilize everything. I need the biology to grow food. But the biology, left to its own devices, will grow things I can't eat. And the things it grows can destroy things I need to survive."

Gabriel absorbed this. He was taking notes without thinking, his recorder app running in the background, capturing not just her words but the pauses, the tone shifts, the moments where her voice tightened.

"Explain it to me," he said. "Not the technical part. The logic part. Why does a closed habitat fear biology?"

Mei set the tablet down and looked at him. Really looked at him, assessing whether this was the right moment for the conversation — and apparently deciding that if there was never a right moment, this one would have to do.

"Closed habitats are paradoxes," she said. "We need living things to survive — microbes, plants, maybe eventually animals — because they do things the machines can't. They convert carbon dioxide to oxygen. They break down waste and return nutrients to the soil. They produce food that isn't just calories but micronutrients, phytonutrients, things that keep a body healthy in ways that synthetic supplements can't fully replicate.

"But the same biology that sustains us can also destroy us." She pointed at the sealed isolation bags stacked against the wall — nine of them now, each containing contaminated growing medium that would need to be treated before it could safely be returned to the compost cycle. "That mold doesn't just kill plants. If it gets into the air system, it could colonize the filters. If it gets into the water recycler, it could compromise the purification membranes. If it gets into the food stores — not the fresh crops, the dry goods, the grain — it could produce mycotoxins. Aflatoxins. Ochratoxins. Substances that don't just spoil food but make it actively poisonous.

"On Earth, you deal with mold by opening a window. You throw away the affected food, you clean the surface, you increase air circulation. The outside air dilutes the contamination, and the problem goes away. Here, we don't have that option. The air in this greenhouse is the same air that circulates through the habitat. What happens here doesn't stay here."

She paused. Took a breath.

"So we're trapped between two impossibilities. We can't have sterile conditions, because sterile conditions mean dead soil, and dead soil means no food. And we can't have natural conditions, because natural conditions on Mars include the slow, persistent pressure of an environment that wants to kill every living thing in this greenhouse. The mold isn't an invader. It's a resident. It's always been here, in the compost, in the seeds, in the cracks between the tiles. I can reduce it. I can manage it. I can fight it. But I can't eliminate it. And neither can you eliminate the desire for oxygen from your own lungs."

Gabriel was quiet for a long moment. The recorder continued to run.

"That's —" he started. Stopped. Started again. "That's one of the most honest things anyone has said about what we're doing here. We're not building a habitat. We're managing a truce."

Mei smiled — barely, more of a grimace than a smile, but genuine. "That's exactly what it is. A negotiated settlement with the microscopic world. And right now, we're losing the negotiation."

---

By midday, the scope of the damage was clear, and the numbers were worse than Mei's first estimate.

The mold — she had sent samples to Laila for identification, and the preliminary diagnosis was *Trichoderma* species, a common soil fungus that was usually beneficial in low concentrations but turned aggressive when the microbial community was out of balance — had spread further than the visual inspection suggested. Microscopic examination of swabs from Rack D revealed hyphae on two additional trays, and one of the trays on Rack A — the cleanest of the four — showed early signs of colonization on a single row of cells.

The contamination was not uniform. It favored the leafy greens — lettuce, spinach, kale — over the brassicas, which made sense given the chemical differences in leaf tissue. Lettuce leaves were thinner, more succulent, easier for fungal hyphae to penetrate. Brassica leaves contained glucosinolates — natural antifungal compounds — that provided some resistance.

But the overall picture was bleak.

Mei stood at the morning board — not the one in the command module, a smaller one she kept in the greenhouse, tracking plant growth stages, nutrient levels, harvest dates — and made the marks that she did not want to make.

Rack B, bottom shelf: clear. Six trays removed. Empty space where green had been.

Rack C, bottom shelf: clear. Three trays removed. One tray treated and quarantined.

Rack D: two trays removed proactively. Four remaining under observation.

Rack A: one tray treated prophylactically. Seven remaining, clean for now.

Total trays lost: fourteen out of twenty-four. More than half. Each tray represented approximately ten days of the thirty-day crop cycle — and because the cycle was staggered, with new trays planted every two to three days, losing trays mid-cycle meant losing the entire harvest window for those crops.

Half a crop cycle. Sacrificed.

Mei wrote it down because writing forced clarity. Fourteen trays lost. Approximately five point six kilograms of biomass destroyed. Twelve days of labor — not just her labor, but the shared support hours from crew members who had helped with watering, monitoring, and general maintenance — consumed with no return.

And the worst part: the cycle could not be simply restarted. The growing medium in the removed trays was contaminated and required treatment — heat sterilization, chemical remediation, and then re-inoculation with the beneficial microbial community — before it could be reused. That process took at least a week. And the physical space on the racks was empty, which meant that even after the medium was clean, there would be a ten-to-fourteen-day gap before replacement plants matured to harvestable size.

She was looking at a loss that extended not just backward — fourteen days of wasted work — but forward. A month at minimum before the greenhouse returned to full production capacity. And during that month, the crew would get even fewer greens than before.

The door chimed. She turned to see Arun standing in the airlock, his expression carefully neutral.

"I got the data from the AI," he said. "Can we talk?"

They sat on the floor of the greenhouse — the only two places to sit were the floor and the edge of the workbench, and the workbench was covered in sampling equipment — and Arun pulled up a spreadsheet on his tablet.

"I ran the numbers," he said. The numbers, always the numbers. "Total greenhouse output before the contamination: approximately six point eight kilograms of fresh greens per week, across all four racks, all cultivars. Projected after remediation — assuming full recovery of clean trays and no further spread — approximately three to three point five kilograms per week. That's a fifty percent reduction in output."

"I know."

"Do you know what that means for the environmental balance? The CO2 enrichment system is calibrated for a certain rate of plant consumption. If the plants are consuming less CO2, the partial pressure will rise. At the current enrichment rate, and with fifty percent fewer plants, the CO2 level will climb by approximately —" he checked the calculator "— one hundred and twenty millipascals over the next forty-eight hours. That takes us above the safe threshold for crew exposure. I'll need to ramp down the enrichment to prevent over-enrichment in the greenhouse."

Mei nodded. "And if you do that, the healthy plants get less CO2, which means they grow more slowly, which means the recovery period extends further."

Arun's expression didn't change, but she saw the slight tightening of his jaw. "Yes."

"So the mold doesn't just cost us greens. It costs us environmental balance, which costs us growth rate, which costs us recovery time. It's not a single loss. It's a cascade."

"Cascades are my specialty," Arun said dryly. "I prefer them on spreadsheets."

---

The confrontation happened at the evening assembly.

It was not dramatic. Mars had taught everyone that dramatic things happened to other people, in other stories. What happened here was quieter and more corrosive: the slow accumulation of frustration in a community where every resource was shared, every choice was political, and every problem demanded labor that nobody had.

Tomas spoke first, which was not surprising — Tomas was the utilities manager, and the utilities systems were where contamination showed up in ways that affected everyone.

"The water recycler needs attention," he said, standing at the front of the common area with his arms crossed. "The mold spores that got into the air — some of them are settling. On surfaces, in the ventilation ducts, and yes, in the water system. Not in the clean water tank — the filters are catching those — but in the grey water loop, where the condensate comes from the greenhouse. I found fungal colonies establishing in two of the condensation collection points. Had to chemically treat both loops. Which means shutting down the condensation recovery for six hours. Which means we lose approximately one hundred liters of reclaimed water that we don't have to spare."

Mei listened. She had expected this. The cascading effects she had warned about were manifesting in real time, and Tomas's anger was justified.

"The air system too," Juno added from her seat near the back. Her voice was tight, controlled. "I've been running the HVAC diagnostics, and the spore load in the return air is elevated. Not dangerously — the HEPA filters are catching the bulk — but enough that I'm seeing colonization on the filter surfaces. I need to replace two filters ahead of schedule. The spare filters are in the environmental stores, and we had budgeted those for the next quarter, not this month."

"Chemical sanitizers," Laila put in. "I've been swabbing high-traffic surfaces as a precaution. The mold is everywhere — not in high concentrations, but it's present. On door handles, on the mess hall tables, on the walls of the corridor outside the greenhouse. I have enough hydrogen peroxide to do a full surface sanitization once, maybe twice. After that, I need a resupply, and we don't have a resupply."

Each voice was a data point, and the data points formed a pattern: the mold was not just a greenhouse problem. It was a colony-wide problem. It affected water, air, labor, chemicals, time.

And every person who described their problem was also, implicitly, asking for labor. Tomas needed help with the chemical treatment. Juno needed two people to assist with filter replacement. Laila needed volunteers for surface sanitization. Mei needed — she had not even started to enumerate her needs, and she could feel the weight of them pressing.

It was Gabriel who named the emotional reality, because that was his job — to articulate the unspoken things that lived between data points.

"Everyone here is angry," he said, not unkindly. "And everyone has a right to be. This isn't just about mold or water or filters. This is about the fact that every person in this colony is already stretched to the limit. We are thirty people doing the work of three hundred. Every unexpected demand — every crisis, every contamination, every cascade — means someone works longer, sleeps less, sacrifices something else. And there is no reservoir of spare capacity to draw from. The reservoir is empty. We've been living on the bottom for months."

"It's my fault," Mei said.

The room went quiet. She spoke without looking up, her eyes on the floor, her hands clasped in front of her.

"Or it isn't. It's nobody's fault, or it's everybody's fault, depending on how you define it. The mold was in the compost. I chose to use that compost because the nutrient profile was right and we didn't have time to process a new batch. I made the trade-off: convenience versus cleanliness. And I chose wrong. Or Mars chose for me, which is the same thing. Either way, the consequence is here, and it's real, and everyone in this room is paying for it."

She looked up. Her face was composed, but her eyes were wet.

"I need help. Not just for the cleanup. For the prevention. I can't manage the microbial balance alone. I need Laila to monitor the pathogen load in the greenhouse as a regular health system. I need Arun to help me design an integrated air quality system that detects spore concentrations before they become visible. I need Tomas to ensure the water recycler has enough antimicrobial capacity to handle the contamination load. I need —" she stopped, swallowed "— I need the colony to stop treating the greenhouse as a separate thing. It's not. It's integrated with everything. The biology in there affects the air, the water, the food, the health of every person. It needs the same level of systemic support that the power grid gets and the water recycler gets and the air scrubbers get."

Silence.

Elena was the first to respond. The commander sat at the back of the room, her hands folded, her expression unreadable. When she spoke, her voice was even and measured.

"You're asking for resources."

"I'm asking for recognition," Mei said. "The biology is not an optional add-on. It's life support. We've been treating it like a nice-to-have — something I manage on my own, with whatever labor I can beg for. But if the biology fails, everything fails. No food. Imbalanced air. Nutrient deficiencies. Psychological degradation. The greenhouse is not separate from the utility infrastructure. It *is* the utility infrastructure."

Another silence. Longer this time.

Tomas shifted in his seat. His arms were still crossed, but the tension in his shoulders had eased slightly.

"I can give you priority access to the chemical treatment system," he said. "For routine sanitization, not just emergencies. But it means delaying the secondary water line inspection by a week."

"I can dedicate two hours per week to pathogen monitoring," Laila said. "Regular swabs, regular lab work, early warning system. But I'll need to shift some of my scheduled patient checkups."

Juno nodded. "I'll add spore concentration sensors to the environmental monitoring suite. It's a software change mostly — the sensors exist, they're just not tuned for biological particles. I can repurpose them."

Arun was quiet. She looked at him. He met her gaze, and after a moment, he nodded.

"I'll model the integrated environment," he said. "Greenhouse, habitat, water, air — all one system. Real-time monitoring, predictive alerts, cascade modeling. If the biology shifts, I want to know before the plants show symptoms."

One by one, the offers came. Not generous — this was Mars, and generosity was measured in hours, not feelings — but they were real. Labor. Time. Attention. Things that each person could barely spare and was choosing to spare anyway.

Mei listened to each one, and with each offer she felt something she had not expected: not relief, not gratitude, but a kind of structural clarity. The mold had forced an argument that needed to happen. The argument about what the greenhouse was, and what the biology was, and how the colony organized itself around the things it needed to survive.

The biology was not a project she ran. It was a system the colony maintained. Together.

The meeting dispersed slowly, the way Mars meetings always did — not with clean resolutions, but with commitments that were specific and limited and would need to be renegotiated in a week or a month or whenever reality diverged from the plan.

Mei stayed seated after everyone left. The recording tablet on her lap was still running — she had not turned it off — and she sat in the quiet, listening to the hum of the greenhouse environmental systems, the circulation fans, the soft electrical buzz of the LED arrays.

The mold was still there. The damage was done. The recovery would take weeks. The losses were real.

But the argument had been had. And the argument had changed something. Not the mold. The politics.

*Biology forces a political argument.*

She stood, put the tablet away, and walked back into the greenhouse to check the plants. The healthy ones still needed tending, and the tending still needed doing, and the work was the work, regardless of what the politics had shifted to in the hour she had spent away from it.

*End of Chapter 22 — Bridge: Biology forces a political argument.*

Arun stood before the food board in the mess hall with a dry-erase marker in his hand and felt the specific, heavy exhaustion of a man who was about to deliver bad news that he had calculated himself and therefore could not blame anyone else for.

The food board was Elena's idea — a physical board, two meters by one, mounted on the wall of the mess hall at eye level, divided into sections. Imported stores on the left. Local production on the right. Consumption in the center. Arrows showing flow. Numbers showing status. The board told the truth about food in a way that a digital report on a tablet never could because a digital report could be closed and ignored and the screen could go dark. The board was always there, catching your eye every time you entered the room to eat whatever the colony had managed to produce that day, reminding you that every meal was a subtraction from a finite total.

Arun updated the board every morning at 0600. It had become a ritual — part of the morning routine that included personal hygiene, a cup of reconstituted something that passed for coffee, and a check of the environmental systems. He erased yesterday's numbers, wrote today's, and stepped back to see what the arithmetic was telling them.

It was telling them what it always told them, with a slight but persistent modification that Arun had been tracking for weeks and had not yet figured out how to communicate in a way that did not cause panic.

The numbers:

**IMPORTED STORES:** 2,400,000 calories (38.7 days)

**GREENHOUSE OUTPUT:** 400 calories/day (0.65% of consumption)

**DAILY CONSUMPTION:** 62,000 calories (30 people x 2,073 avg)

**VARIANCE:** +400/-62,000

**ADJUSTED DEPLETION:** 39.3 days

The greenhouse was producing four hundred calories per day. Four hundred. Out of sixty-two thousand needed. The math was not cruel — math was nothing, it had no intention — but the result of the math was cruel. It said that the greenhouse, for all its emotional significance, its psychological necessity, its undeniable beauty, was not feeding anyone yet. It was feeding the *idea* of feeding. Which mattered, but not in the way that calories mattered.

Arun finished writing the numbers and stepped back. The board looked the same as it had yesterday — almost the same. The imported stores number had dropped by three hundred calories, which was a rounding error, and the greenhouse number had increased by fifty, which was also a rounding error. The arrow between them, the one that represented the gap between what they had and what they needed, had not moved.

People were starting to filter into the mess hall for breakfast. Breakfast on Mars was usually reconstituted protein paste — the kind that came in sealed silver pouches, labeled with barcodes and nutritional information and manufactured somewhere Arun didn't think about anymore because the more he thought about the factories and supply chains and people on Earth who no longer thought about the things they had helped create, the harder it was to eat with any intention beyond calorie intake.

Juno was first, as usual. She had a system: eat fast, eat efficiently, get back to the console. She grabbed her pouch, saw the board, and did a double-take.

"Thirty-eight days?"

"Thirty-nine point three, accounting for greenhouse supplementation," Arun corrected. "It changed by about half a day since I last updated. The math has a half-day resolution. It's not enough to celebrate."

"I wasn't going to celebrate."

"I know. I'm telling you anyway."

She read the board the way she read medical charts — scanning, absorbing, cross-referencing against her own data.

"The greenhouse is only four hundred calories?" she asked, not accusatory, genuinely seeking.

"Four hundred," Arun confirmed. "About one percent. It provides micronutrients, it provides morale, it provides —" he glanced toward the greenhouse corridor "— it provides things that are not calories but are necessary. A salad can make a person feel human again, Laila. But it cannot yet carry thirty people through a month, let alone a winter."

She nodded slowly. She understood nutrition. She also understood the difference between what a body needed chemically and what a mind needed existentially. The greenhouse provided the latter, barely, and not the former, not yet.

"The imported vitamins are degrading too," she said quietly. "The shelf life of the synthetic supplements is finite, and we're past the halfway point. The degradation curve is exponential — they lose more potency each month than the month before. In six months, what you're getting from a vitamin pill is less than thirty percent of what the label says. Eventually, it's nothing. Just a pill that tastes like disappointment."

"I hate those pills too," Arun said. "But they're all we have until the greenhouse produces enough variety to cover the full micronutrient profile. And that requires the expansion. Which requires labor. Which requires time we're not sure we have."

---

The conversation that Arun needed to have — the one that was coming whether he was ready or not — started three hours later, in the command module, with Elena at the desk and half the senior staff standing or sitting wherever they could find space.

Mei was there, obviously — this was about the greenhouse, and the greenhouse was her domain. She stood near the desk, tablet in hand, her expression determined in a way that Arun had learned to recognize. Determination from Mei was different from determination from most people. Most people's determination was emotional — a willpower thing. Mei's determination was mathematical. She had calculated something, and the calculation was driving the emotion, not the other way around.

Jonah sat in the back, his arms crossed, his face blank. Jonah's blankness was not indifference — it was the face of a man who was listening to other people talk about things that he would eventually need to build, and he was already cataloging the requirements in his head.

Tomas was there — utilities, always utilities — and Laila, and Juno, and Arun himself, who was the person responsible for translating Mei's biological ambitions into the hard numbers of energy, water, and labor that made those ambitions either possible or fantasy.

Elena opened the discussion without preamble, the way she always did.

"We need to talk about food," she said. "Arun updated the board this morning. Thirty-nine days of imported calories. The greenhouse is at four hundred per day. The gap is real and it is getting larger, not smaller, every time the board updates. Mei, tell me what you need to close it."

Mei was ready. She had prepared a document — not a presentation, just a simple one-page summary, the kind of document that engineers and scientists used when they knew the executives in the room would not have time for slides.

"Expansion into calorie crops," she said, distributing copies of the sheet. "The current greenhouse is optimized for leafy greens — fast-cycle, high-nutrient, low-calorie crops. She turned to a second page, a floor plan.

"I need wheat. Potatoes. Dry beans. Soybeans. Sweet potatoes, if I can get the tuber development working — the lower gravity makes root development tricky, but the literature suggests it's possible with the right soil structure and moisture management. These crops have longer cycles — ninety to one hundred twenty days from planting to harvest, compared to thirty for the leafy greens — but the caloric yield per square meter is orders of magnitude higher."

Mei nodded. She knew this dance. They had done it before — during the initial greenhouse design, during the first expansion planning session — and the rhythm was familiar.

Beans: four thousand per square meter, two harvests, ninety-six thousand annually."
