Plus ongoing maintenance: approximately eight person-hours per day across all crops once operational."

"Two hundred thirty person-hours," Elena repeated. She was doing the math in her head — she was good at mental math, a skill she had developed in university and sharpened in three years of command. "With the current labor allocation — four person-hours per day per non-critical crew member — that's approximately fifty-eight person-hours per week. So four weeks of parallel work by four people. But we can't assign four people full-time to this because they have other jobs that also need doing."

"Correct," Arun said. "We're looking at six to eight weeks of part-time labor spread across multiple crew members. During which time, the people working on the greenhouse expansion are not working on whatever else they would have been doing."

That was the gap. The labor gap. The thing that every plan on Mars eventually came to — the simple, brutal, inescapable fact that the colony had thirty people and more work than thirty people could do, and every new project meant an old project going slower or stopping.

The question was always the same: what project stops so the greenhouse can grow?

Elena asked it before anyone else could, because she had learned that asking the hard question first was better than letting it float unasked until it poisoned the room.

"What project loses labor so farming can gain it?" she asked. Her voice was quiet. The question was not a challenge. It was an acknowledgment that every choice has a cost, and the cost is always measured in the work that does not get done.

Nobody answered immediately. The silence was the sound of people running the inventory of their responsibilities and calculating the price of their own time.

Tomas spoke first, reluctantly. "The water system. I was planning to do a full diagnostic of the grey water loop next week — check all the membranes, flush the filters, run a chemical analysis of each stage. It's scheduled maintenance, not emergency. It can wait — for a while. But the longer it waits, the higher the risk of a failure that becomes an emergency. I can defer it by two weeks, maybe three. After that, the degradation of the filtration membranes crosses a threshold, and I need to replace them preemptively, which would pull me off the greenhouse entirely."

"I have the secondary air scrubber installation scheduled," Juno said. "It's been on the list for three months. The primary scrubber is fine for now, but the secondary is redundancy, and redundancy is the difference between a manageable maintenance event and a crisis if the primary fails. I can push it back by a month. Maybe two. But I don't want the primary failing while the secondary is still in its crate."

"Medical —" Laila started.

"You don't give up medical," Elena said immediately. Not unkindly — as a statement of fact. Medical was the one area of the colony that did not negotiate. The health of thirty people was not a line item; it was the foundation on which all other line items rested.

"Agreed," Laila said. "I don't give up medical. But I can reduce my greenhouse monitoring hours temporarily — shift some of my scheduled patient wellness checks, consolidate them. It means less individual attention for each person, but I can still monitor the critical metrics."

"Fabrication," Jonah said. He had been quiet, leaning against the wall, his arms crossed, his eyes on the ceiling as if calculating the load-bearing capacity of a structural beam that existed only in his imagination.

"Jonah?" Elena prompted.

Jonah looked down. His face was still blank — the blankness of someone who has been thinking about one thing for a very long time and is now being asked to switch to another.

"The machine yard," he said. "The parts we've been salvaging from the old landers and the decommissioned equipment. The stuff we pulled out of the rovers when the rovers failed and we couldn't fix them. I've been cataloging it — sorting, grading, cleaning, storing. It's slow work, and it doesn't produce anything you can use right now. It produces the possibility of future use. A gear from a rover motor might be the exact size we need for a greenhouse ventilation fan. A bearing from a solar tracker might be exactly what the water pump needs. But I only know that after I've cleaned it, measured it, and cataloged it. And the cataloging process takes hours per part."

He stood up. The movement was deliberate, the way a man moves when he has decided something and is now presenting the decision as information, not as a request.

"I can shift the cataloging to maintenance-only mode," Jonah said. "Sort the obvious stuff — the large components, the easily identified parts — and set aside the rest for later. It means we lose the detailed catalog, which means we lose the ability to find specific parts quickly when we need them. But it frees up approximately fifteen hours per week. Fifteen hours that I can put into building the greenhouse frames instead of cataloging the parts that might be used to build them someday."

Elena looked at him for a long moment. "Jonah, if we lose that catalog, and a critical system fails, and the part we need was in the pile you didn't catalog —"

"Then we find it when we need it," Jonah said. "We dig. It'll take longer, and the part might be buried, but it'll be there. The parts don't go away. The time does."

He was right. And he knew he was right, which was why Elena could see the slight tension in his jaw — the tension of a man who was making a professional compromise he did not want to make and was presenting it anyway because the alternative — not making it — was worse.

---

The meeting continued for another forty minutes, with each person in the room identifying what they could defer, what they could compress, what they could hand off to someone else, what they could simply stop doing. By the end, Elena had a rough labor allocation plan: Mei would lead the greenhouse expansion, with Jonah providing fabrication support, Arun handling the electrical and environmental hookups, and two additional crew members — Imani and Wei, pulled from construction duty — providing general labor.

It was not enough labor to do the work quickly. It was enough to do it, slowly, over six to eight weeks, during which time other projects would decelerate or pause entirely.

The cost was real. The benefit would be real too, but in a language that was harder to measure: the difference between thirty-nine days of imported food and eventually, someday, not needing the imported food at all. The difference between farming as an experiment and farming as a lifeline.

"We'll start on Monday," Elena said, closing the meeting. "Mei, I want a detailed construction plan from you by Friday. Jonah, start pulling materials today — aluminum struts, LED fixtures, irrigation components. Arun, run the power projections — I need to know that the greenhouse won't overload the grid once the LED arrays are running. Tomas, begin your water system diagnostic tomorrow, before it gets deferred. Make sure the system is solid going into the expansion period. Laila, set up your reduced monitoring schedule and send it to me for review."

Everyone nodded. Everyone had their assignment. The plan existed — not as a finished document, but as a set of commitments that would be tested, revised, and tested again as reality asserted itself.

As the room emptied, Arun lingered. He stayed because he had one more conversation to have, and it was a conversation that did not belong in the larger meeting because it was about something that the larger group was not ready to acknowledge.

"Mei," he said. She was at the door, tablet in hand, preparing to return to the greenhouse.

She turned. "Yeah."

"The greenhouse expansion will help, but it's not enough."

"I know."

"No, I mean —" He hesitated. Then he decided to be direct, because Mei respected directness even when the directness was unpleasant. "The greenhouse expansion, even with forty-eight square meters of calorie crops, even with the best-case yield projections, produces approximately three hundred twenty-four thousand calories per year. That's approximately eleven hundred calories per day. We need sixty-two thousand. Eleven hundred is not enough. It's not even close to enough."

"I know," Mei said again. Her voice was flat, the voice of someone who had already had this conversation with herself.

"What I'm saying is that the greenhouse will never carry the colony alone. The greenhouse is a supplement. It will always be a supplement, unless we build an area the size of the habitat itself. And we can't do that. Not with the resources we have. We will always need some combination of imported stores and local production. The question is how much of each, and at what point the balance shifts from mostly-imported to mostly-local."

"When?" Mei asked. It was the question she had been avoiding, the question that every optimistic projection eventually confronted.

"Based on the current growth rate of the colony — and assuming the birth rate stays at what Laila says is plausible, which is low, because pregnancy on Mars is complicated and we're being cautious — based on a population growing by maybe two to three per year, we need an additional fifty thousand calories per year per birth. If the greenhouse produces three hundred twenty-four thousand per year and the population grows by two — plus one hundred thousand in demand — we need to expand again. Within two years. And again within the year after. The greenhouse will need to grow at least as fast as the population, and probably faster, because we also need to increase per-capita nutrition as the colony stabilizes and moves from survival to something that looks like thriving."

Mei absorbed this. The numbers were not discouraging — they were clarifying. They said that the greenhouse was not a one-time project. It was a permanent, growing, expanding commitment that the colony would need to sustain for as long as the colony existed.

"I need to plan for that," she said finally. "Not just the first expansion. The second, the third, the ongoing trajectory. Not as a series of individual projects, but as a system. An agricultural system that grows with the colony."

"Yes," Arun said. "But also — and this is the part I wanted to say privately, because I didn't want to say it in front of Elena — you need to be honest about what the greenhouse can and cannot do. People are going to look at those first trays of wheat and potatoes and see salvation. They're not salvation. They're a step. An important step. But a step, not an arrival. If you promise more than the greenhouse can deliver, even implicitly, even by not setting expectations clearly, you create a different kind of starvation — emotional starvation, the kind that comes from hope colliding with arithmetic."

Mei was quiet. She looked at the food board one more time — the numbers she had not written, the numbers Arun had written, the gap between them that would close slowly, incrementally, over years of work.

"I'll be honest," she said. "I always am. Even when the honesty means telling people that the thing they most need to believe in is not big enough yet."

"Honesty is a resource too," Arun said. "Like seed stock. Use it carefully, but use it. Because the colony that is lied to about its food situation is the colony that doesn't prepare for the situation it's actually in."

She nodded. They stood together for a moment longer — the engineer and the farmer, the number-keeper and the plant-tender, two people who had learned to speak each other's languages across the gap between biology and systems — and then they separated, each returning to their own domain, each carrying the weight of work that was necessary and insufficient and would need to be done again tomorrow.

Arun walked back to the mess hall to update the board one more time. The numbers had not changed in the two hours since he had written them. The gap was the same. The arrow was the same.

But as he stood in front of the board, marker in hand, he thought about what Jonah had said about the machine yard. About the cataloged parts, the salvaged components, the broken machines that held within them the seeds of future solutions. About how every problem on Mars eventually came back to the same resources: labor, time, materials, and the will to redistribute them toward the things that mattered most.

Broken machines became food's hidden cost.

Arun erased a number, wrote it again, and stepped back to let the board continue telling its quiet, persistent, inescapable story.

But without the antibiotics working — without shutting down the source of the inflammatory response — the cooling is cosmetic. I need the antibiotics to work."

She checked the blood culture results. No growth yet — the bacteria needed more time, and time was the one resource she was running out of.

At 17:42, Youssef's breathing changed.

The change was subtle at first — the rhythm shifted, his breaths became irregular, with periods of rapid breathing interspersed with pauses. Laila recognized the pattern immediately: Cheyne-Stokes respiration. A sign of central nervous system compromise, of the brain's respiratory center beginning to fail, of the body's most fundamental automatic function — breathing — losing its coordination.

She leaned close to him. "Youssef. Can you hear me? Squeeze my hand if you can hear me."

His right hand — the one not in the IV — moved slowly and closed around her fingers. The grip was weak, too weak, but it was present.

"I'm here," she said. Her voice was steady, but the steadiness was the kind of performance that cost something. "I'm right here."

His hand tightened. Then released. Then tightened again, weaker this time.

The monitor beeped — not the rapid, alarming alarm of cardiac arrest, but the slow, persistent tone of deteriorating perfusion. Blood pressure: 68 over 40. Heart rate: 148. Lactate: 7.4.

Laila made a decision. She increased the norepinephrine dose — pushing it toward the maximum recommended level — and called for Elena again.

Elena arrived. The space at the foot of the bed was beginning to feel like the center of a room where all the gravity was concentrated.

"He's declining," Laila said. "The antibiotics haven't worked yet — lactate is rising, blood pressure is falling, breathing pattern is changing to Cheyne-Stokes. I've maxed the vasopressor dose. Unless there's a response in the next hour —" She stopped.

"Unless what?" Elena asked, though she knew.

"Unless the antibiotics start working, I can't stop the progression. I can slow it — fluids, pressors, cooling, oxygen — but the underlying process is independent of my interventions. It's determined by whether the organism is sensitive to the drugs I gave and whether the dose was sufficient and whether his body can mount an immune response that cooperates with the treatment instead of accelerating the damage."

"How long?"

Laila thought carefully. In medicine, time estimates were the most dangerous kind of prediction because they implied a certainty that did not exist. But Elena needed numbers, and Laila was not the kind of physician who refused to give numbers because they were uncomfortable.

"If the antibiotics are going to work, I should see improvement in the next hour. Maybe ninety minutes. Blood pressure rising without additional pressor. Lactate trending down. Temperature stabilizing. If I don't see those signs by six-thirty —" She checked the clock. 17:52. "— by six-thirty, I would consider the empirical treatment a failure. And I don't have a good second-line option. The remaining antibiotics are narrower-spectrum. If the organism doesn't respond to pip-tazo and vancomycin, it's unlikely to respond to anything else I have."

Elena was quiet. She looked at Youssef — his chest rising and falling in the irregular Cheyne-Stokes pattern, his face swollen from the fluid shift, his hand open on the table, the IV line running clear into his arm, the monitor painting his decline in digital numbers that everyone in the room could read.

"Can I talk to him?" she asked.

Laila nodded. "He was responsive a few minutes ago. I can't guarantee he'll track now, but — yes. He can hear you. Hearing is the last thing to go."

Elena moved to Youssef's side. She knelt beside the table — not because she needed to, but because kneeling put her at his eye level, and eye level was the level where a commander stopped being a commander and became a person talking to another person who was crossing a threshold.

"Youssef," she said. "I'm Elena. I'm right here."

His eyes opened. They were glassy, fever-bright, the pupils slightly dilated. But they found her face. Recognition, flickering, fading, returning.

"I can hear you," he whispered. The words were barely audible. "Laila — is she — are you doing — everything?"

"Yes," Laila said from her position at the foot of the bed. "Everything."

"Good." A pause. The breathing pattern continued — rapid breaths, pause, rapid breaths. "Tell Amara — tell her the buildings — I built them strong. Like I told her. On Earth. I told her I would build strong things. These —" He tried to gesture and couldn't. His hand barely twitched. "These are strong. Tell her."

"I'll tell her," Elena said. The promise again. The contract. "She'll know. I promise."

He closed his eyes. The breathing continued. The monitor continued. Laila continued — adjusting the IV, checking the pressor flow, monitoring the temperature, the blood pressure, the saturations, the lactate, every number a data point in a dataset she was already beginning to interpret in the way she did not want to interpret it.

The numbers were telling the story. She just didn't want to read the last page.

---

At 18:17, the monitor alarmed.

Not blood pressure. Not oxygen. Heart rhythm. The screen displayed a pattern Laila recognized before the alarm finished its first tone: ventricular tachycardia — a fast, abnormal rhythm originating from the heart's lower chambers, the kind of rhythm that preceded cardiac arrest if the cause was not corrected quickly.

"Youssef," Laila said sharply, leaning over him. "Can you hear me?"

No response. His eyes were open but not focused. The Cheyne-Stokes pattern had been replaced by something worse — agonal breathing, the gasping, irregular, desperate pattern of a brain stem that was beginning to shut down, firing off the last signals it could produce to a body that was no longer responding.

"Ventricular tachycardia," she said, speaking for the log, speaking for the record, speaking for the version of this moment that would exist in the permanent archive and would be read by people who were not born yet. "Heart rate 178, irregular rhythm. Blood pressure non-palpable. Patient unconscious."

She pushed the code cart to the bedside — the small wheeled unit that contained the tools of cardiac resuscitation: a defibrillator, emergency medications, an airway kit, and the things you used when a person's heart was beating wrong and needed it to beat right.

"Youssef," she said, because the person always mattered more than the rhythm. Because the first step in resuscitation was always to confirm unresponsiveness, and confirmation required the human act of speaking to someone and waiting for a reply.

No reply.

She activated the defibrillator. Charged to 200 joules. Applied the pads to Youssef's chest — one on the upper right, one on the lower left, the standard placement for biphasic defibrillation.

"Clear," she said.

The shock went in. Youssef's body arched slightly — the involuntary muscular contraction of the current passing through the chest — and then settled. The monitor displayed a flat line for one second. Two seconds. Then the rhythm returned.

Sinus rhythm. For three beats.

Then back to ventricular tachycardia. Different morphology this time — faster, wider, more disorganized. The electrical signal in his heart was becoming chaotic.

*Second shock. 200 joules. Clear. Shock delivered.*

Sinus rhythm. For two beats.

Ventricular fibrillation. The worst rhythm. The electrical signal was no longer even trying to organize itself. The heart was quivering, a bag of muscle fibers each contracting independently, producing no cardiac output at all.

Laila began compressions. Her hands on his sternum, pressing at the recommended depth — five to six centimeters — at the recommended rate — one hundred to one hundred twenty compressions per minute — the mechanical act of squeezing the heart between the breastbone and the spine to maintain some degree of blood flow to the brain and vital organs.

On Earth, this was a team sport. Compressors alternating every two minutes. Airway management by a second person. IV medications by a third. Rhythm analysis by a fourth. On Mars, it was one woman, thirty-four years old, from Lagos, a structural engineer who had built things for his daughter, and the physician who was now pressing on his chest in a medical bay that had everything she needed except the one thing that mattered: time.

She compressed. Counted under her breath. *One, two, three, four, five* — her arms straight, her shoulders directly above her hands, the mechanical efficiency of a CPR technique she had practiced hundreds of times on manikins and once, briefly, on a person in a Lagos emergency room who had survived.

"Epinephrine, one milligram IV," she said, grabbing the syringe from the code cart and pushing it into the IV port. A drug that tightened blood vessels and stimulated the heart's electrical system, trying to coax it back into a rhythm that could sustain life.

She continued compressions. The rhythm on the monitor was changing — fibrillation to asystole. No electrical activity at all. Flatline.

"Continue compressions. Second dose of epinephrine in three minutes."

She compressed. Her arms were tired. CPR at the recommended depth and rate for an adult required physical effort — a sustained, maximal output that exhausted even fit people within minutes. She was fit. She was also three hours into treating a patient who was deteriorating despite her best efforts, and the exhaustion she felt was not just physical.

Three minutes passed. She checked the rhythm. Asystole. Flatline. She gave the second epinephrine dose. Continued compressions.

Five minutes. Ten minutes. Fifteen.

Youssef's blood pressure on the monitor — generated only by her compressions — was 40 over 20. Just enough to perfuse the brain, barely. His pupils were fixed and dilated. The Cheyne-Stokes breathing had stopped. The agonal breathing had stopped. He was not breathing at all. She was the one breathing for him, with a bag-valve mask between compressions, squeezing the bag to force air into his lungs.

Twenty minutes.

She stopped compressions. Checked the rhythm. Asystole. No change.

She looked at the clock. 18:44. Youssef had been in cardiac arrest for twenty-one minutes. On Earth, the standard recommendation was to stop resuscitation after twenty to thirty minutes if there was no return of spontaneous circulation. The neurological outcome after more than fifteen minutes of cardiac arrest was almost universally poor, even with immediate, high-quality CPR.

Here, on Mars, with the resources she had, the standard was different. There was no standard. There was only the woman beside the table, her arms shaking, her heart pounding, her brain telling her the numbers and her hands refusing to stop.

She resumed compressions.

Twenty-five minutes.

She stopped. Checked the rhythm. Asystole. She checked for a pulse — nothing, just the cold, smooth skin of a man her compressions had kept alive by mechanical force but whose heart had no intention of restarting.

She looked at the monitor one more time. Flatline. No electrical activity. No cardiac output. No breath. No response. Just the line, horizontal, extending to the right without deviation, the simplest and most final graphic in medicine.

She stopped compressions.

"Time of death," she said, "eighteen forty-seven station time. Station Day 734."

She stepped away from the table. Her hands were shaking. She held them in front of her, looking at them — the hands that had done everything a physician could do with the tools available — IV, antibiotics, fluids, pressors, defibrillation, compressions — and had not been enough.

Not because she was incompetent. Because the infection was too fast, the organism too aggressive, the supply too limited, the planet too far from the things she needed.

She sat on the stool beside the table, removed her gloves, and stared at Youssef's face.

He looked peaceful. The swelling from the fluid shift had given his face a soft appearance that almost looked like sleep. His eyes were closed. His mouth was slightly open. The oxygen cannula had been removed. The IV was still in place, the saline line running into nothing — the body that had been receiving it no longer had circulation, and the fluid was pooling in the tissues, slowly, imperceptibly, doing nothing.

Laila reached over and clamped the IV line. A small gesture. The kind of gesture a medical professional makes when the medical part is done — turning off the machines that no longer serve the person they were serving, because it is a kindness to stop the interventions that the dead body no longer needs.

She sat. The medical bay was quiet — the only sound was the faint hum of the air recirculation system and the distant, always-present sound of the habitat keeping thirty minus one people alive.

She had lost a patient. The first patient she had lost on Mars. Probably not the last, if septic infections were going to be a thing that happened in closed environments with finite medical supplies. But the first one. The first one was always the one that changed the physician.

---

The death was not shocking. That was the thing about it that made it worse, in a way Laila could not fully articulate.

It was not shocking because everyone had seen it coming. The crew had watched Youssef stumble in Tunnel B. They had watched him lean on Laila's shoulder as they walked to the medical bay. They had gathered outside the medical bay door during the first hour, drawn by the alert tone, the urgency in Laila's voice on the comm, the way people who live together in an enclosed space move toward disturbance the way water moves toward a crack.

They had stood in the corridor and listened. Heard the monitor alarms. Heard Laila's voice, steady and professional, calling out numbers and orders and drug names. Heard the silence that followed the silence too many times, the kind of silence that has weight because it is the sound of a person who is doing everything they can and knowing it is not enough.

And then, at 18:47, Laila's voice on the comm, quiet, clear, final: "Youssef Diallo, deceased. Station Day 734, time eighteen forty-seven."

No shock. Just the landing of something that had been falling for three hours.

Jonah was the first to speak in the corridor. He stood beside Arun, both of them having put down their tools and come running when the first alert sounded.

"It was the arm," Jonah said. Not a question. An assessment. "The surgery. The hardware. Something in the bone."

"Maybe," Arun said. "Or maybe it was something else. We don't know yet. The blood culture should identify —" He stopped. The blood culture was in the incubator. Youssef was dead. The culture would still produce a result in forty hours, but the result would be an answer to a question that no longer had practical importance.

"Told me it could happen," Jonah said quietly. "After the surgery. When I made the plate and the screws. Told Laila they were as clean as I could make them. As clean as the shop could be. But the shop isn't a clean room. The metal isn't sterilized to surgical standards. The plate — the plate I made for his arm — if there was a single bacterium on it, in the bone —" He stopped. His voice was flat, the voice of a man running through causal chains that, on Mars, had a way of extending further than anyone wanted them to.

"It's not your fault, Jonah," Arun said. He said it without conviction because conviction required certainty, and certainty did not exist in causal chains on Mars.

"I know," Jonah said. He did not believe it. He also could not disbelieve it. And the tension between those two states — knowing and not knowing — was the state in which the colony had existed since landing: building things that might fail because they had to build things, and living with the consequences when the things failed because they had.

Mei arrived last. She had been in the greenhouse, monitoring the mold remediation progress, and she had heard the alert on her comm but had not been able to leave immediately — the plants required attention whether the medical bay was busy or not, and the discipline of tending to the living while the dying was happening elsewhere was a discipline that felt inhuman and necessary simultaneously.

She stood in the corridor, looking at the closed door of the medical bay, and she knew. She knew because the crew's posture told her it — the way people stood with their shoulders slightly forward, their arms crossed or their hands in their pockets, the collective body language of a group that had received news and was processing it in silence.

She did not ask. She knew.

Tomas was there, his face the color of the regolith outside — pale, drawn, the face of a man who had lost a crew member and was already calculating the labor deficit that the loss created. Four rovers instead of four active people. Three instead of three. The math did not care about grief. The math was the math.

And Elena stood at the head of the corridor, not moving. The commander. The person who had looked Youssef in the eye hours ago and promised to deliver a message to his daughter. The person who would now have to decide what happened to the body, how the colony would respond, how twenty-nine people would carry the weight of the first death in their community.

The task that killed Youssef had been routine. That was the hardest part. He had not been on a dangerous EVA. He had not been exploring unknown terrain or conducting a high-risk repair or working at the edge of the habitat's safety envelope. He had been doing something he had done a thousand times before — walking through a tunnel, carrying a tool, heading from one work station to another — and his body, compromised by an infection that had been growing quietly for weeks or months, had simply failed. The stumble, the shortness of breath, the rapid decline — all of it caused by something that had been present in his body long before anyone noticed it, long before Laila's analyzers could detect it, long before it became the thing that killed him.

It was the kind of death that had no drama and no warning. A person walking through a tunnel, his immune system losing a war he did not know he was fighting, until the war became a collapse and the collapse became a cardiac arrest and the arrest became a flatline.

Everyone could see how normal the task had seemed. That was what made the death land hardest. Not the shock. The normalness of it. The fact that Youssef had done nothing dangerous, taken no risks, accepted no unusual exposure — he had simply been doing the work and the work had been what it was on Mars: the accumulation of small, invisible risks that eventually found the weakness and exploited it.

---

Elena sat in the command module for forty-seven minutes after the death was announced. She did not issue orders. She did not call a meeting. She sat in the darkness with only the blue light of the terminal screen and she let herself think about what came next.

The body was in the medical bay. Laila had covered it with a sheet — a clean sheet, not a body bag, because the colony did not have body bags and because a sheet felt more human. The sheet draped over Youssef's face and torso, leaving nothing visible except the outline of his body beneath the fabric, the slight irregularity where his chest should have been rising and was not.

The question was: what to do with the body?

On Earth, the answer was simple. Hospitals had morgues. Morticians had protocols. Cemeteries had plots. Families had wishes. The infrastructure of death was as well-developed as the infrastructure of life, and every society had a ritual for moving from one state to the other.

On Mars, there was no infrastructure of death. There was a medical bay with a sheet on a table and a colony that had never had to do this before.

Elena ran the options through her mind, evaluating each one against the colony's constraints: space, energy, materials, time, and sentiment.

**Option one: preserve the body.** Store it in the cryogenic freezer that was currently used for biological samples and food preservation. Remove the samples, make space, cool the body to minus eighty Celsius, and wait — wait for what? For a return mission that might never come? For a repatriation that was not on anyone's calendar? The space cost was significant. The energy cost was ongoing — the freezer consumed power continuously, and power was committed to other essential systems. And the psychological cost — living alongside a frozen crew member, walking past the freezer every day, knowing what was inside — that cost was incalculable.

**Option two: burial in the regolith.** Dig a grave. On Mars, digging required a rover or an EVA — both of which had costs. The body would need to be wrapped, transported through the airlock, and placed in a location far enough from the habitat that it would not interfere with operations but close enough that the crew could visit if they wanted. The regolith was permafrost in places, which meant the body would remain preserved indefinitely — not decomposing, not returning to the carbon cycle, just existing in the cold as a frozen thing in frozen ground. The energy cost of the burial EVA was modest but real. The psychological benefit of a ritual — of a moment where the crew collectively acknowledged the loss and the person — was significant.

**Option three: cremation.** Not technically possible with the colony's current infrastructure. The power required to cremate a body was enormous — several hundred kilowatt-hours — and the habitat did not have a furnace designed for that purpose. Building one would require fabrication time, materials, and a commitment of resources that the colony could not easily spare. Option three was off the table.

**Option four: airlock ejection.** Putting the body in the airlock and opening the outer door. Letting Mars take what Mars had already claimed. The energy cost was minimal — one airlock cycle, approximately four kilowatt-hours. The space cost was zero. The psychological cost, however, was enormous. Ejection felt like disposal. And Youssef Diallo was not waste. He was a person who had built the structures that kept twenty-nine others alive. Disposing of him through an airlock would feel like discarding the very thing Elena had spent two years trying to honor: the human labor that made Mars habitable.

She eliminated option one and option three immediately — one was logistically possible but psychologically damaging, the other was technologically impossible. That left option two and option four: burial or ejection.

Burial required labor. A rover, an EVA crew, the digging equipment, the wrapping materials, the time. It required the colony to invest resources — scarce, precious, already-committed resources — in a ritual that produced nothing but meaning.

Ejection required resources in the opposite direction: it saved resources, conserved labor, and treated the body as mass to be discarded. It was the efficiency-maximizing option. It was also the option that would make the crew feel like Youssef had been garbage.

Elena closed her eyes. The question was not really about burial versus ejection. The question was about what the colony was. Was it a utility — a collection of systems and people and resources optimized for survival, where every decision was evaluated against the metric of caloric efficiency and energy balance? Or was it a community — a group of people who needed rituals and meaning and the acknowledgment that their losses mattered, even when the losses cost more than they could afford?

On Earth, the answer was both. You had the practical systems for dealing with the dead — the mortuaries, the cemeteries, the crematoriums — and you had the rituals, the ceremonies, the words spoken over the body, the moments of shared grief. The practical systems existed so the rituals could happen.

On Mars, the colony had neither. And Elena had to choose which one to build first.

She thought about Youssef's daughter. Amara. Nine years old, somewhere on Earth, a child whose father had told her he was building strong things. Elena had promised to tell her about the buildings. She had not promised to bring him home.

She made the decision.

She opened her comm and keyed the all-hands channel.

"All crew members. Briefing in the mess hall at 0700 tomorrow — Station Day 735. Topic: Youssef Diallo's memorial and interment. Attendance is voluntary but recommended."

She closed the channel. The decision was made. They would do the burial. A ritual. A moment. A cost in labor and time that the colony could not easily afford, because the cost of not doing it — the cost of reducing Youssef to ejected mass — was higher.

Tomorrow they would discuss the logistics. Tomorrow they would allocate the rover time, the EVA crew, the materials. Tomorrow they would bury one of their own in the regolith of a world that had not asked for them and would not remember them.

But tonight, Elena sat in the dark and let herself feel the thing that the briefings and logistics and allocations would not allow tomorrow.

One of theirs was gone. The first. The one who had built strong things and whose body had failed anyway because Mars amplified every weakness and the infection had been invisible until it was everything.

She sat with it. The weight of it. The normalness of it. The terrible, ordinary, unavoidable truth that on another world, the price of being alive was higher than anyone had calculated, and the invoice came due without warning.

---

Gabriel sat in the communications alcove at 0300, three hours after the death, writing in the Founding Record.

The Record was his responsibility. It was the permanent, searchable archive of the colony's history — every event, every decision, every technical specification, every birth and injury and system failure documented with the care of a historian building something that would outlast the people who created it. He had been writing the Record since Sol 1, and the entries had grown from technical observations — *atmospheric pressure nominal, power generation on schedule* — to something richer, something that captured not just what happened but what it meant.

Tonight's entry was the hardest one he had written.

He started with the facts.

*Station Day 734. Time 18:47. Youssef Diallo, 34, structural engineer, Lagos, died of septic shock secondary to presumed bloodstream infection. Symptoms presented at 14:23. Treated aggressively by Dr. Laila Okonkwo with IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin), supplemental oxygen, vasopressors, and attempted cardiac resuscitation. Return of spontaneous circulation not achieved. Time of death: 18:47.*

He paused. The facts were necessary but insufficient. The Record was not a hospital chart. It was a document that would be read by people who needed to understand not just what happened but why it mattered.

He continued.

*Youssef Diallo was a member of the founding crew. He was responsible for the structural integrity of the habitat's load-bearing systems, the fabrication and installation of critical support hardware, and fourteen successful EVAs. He survived a work-related injury on Day 437 — a comminuted fracture of the left forearm caused by a manufactured bolt failure — and returned to full duty on Day 512 after successful surgical repair by Dr. Okonkwo. His contributions to the colony include the greenhouse support structures, the airlock reinforcement, the secondary hab connection, and the fabrication of titanium surgical hardware used in his own arm repair.*

*He had a daughter on Earth. Amara Diallo, age nine. He carried a photograph of her in his bunk — a small printed image, laminated against moisture damage, showing a girl with dark hair and a gap-toothed smile standing in front of a building he had designed for her school. He showed the photograph to crew members who asked about his life before Mars, and he spoke about her with the particular pride of a person whose child existed in a world he had left behind and whose future he was helping to build from the other side of space.*

Gabriel stopped writing. His hands were steady — they were always steady when he wrote, because the act of writing was a discipline, the same discipline that had made him the colony's chronicler — but his chest felt tight, the feeling of a man recording something he needed to record but did not want to.

He continued.

*Youssef died not during a dangerous operation but during ordinary movement through the habitat. He was walking from the fabrication bay to the habitat core when he stumbled and was noticed to be pale, breathless, and febrile. The infection had been progressing silently — for days, weeks, possibly months — at a level below clinical detection. By the time symptoms appeared, the infection was already in the bloodstream, triggering a systemic inflammatory response that overwhelmed his cardiovascular system.*

*There was no failure of procedure. No negligence. No avoidable error. Laila Okonkwo followed the standard protocol for septic shock, administering fluids, antibiotics, vasopressors, and resuscitation within minutes of identification. The treatment was appropriate. The outcome was not guaranteed.*

*The organism has not yet been identified. Blood cultures are in incubation. The colony will learn the name of what killed Youssef Diallo in approximately forty hours. It will learn the name but not how it got there — whether from the surgical site, from the environment, from a dormant organism activated by stress, from a thousand possible pathways that lead from invisible to fatal in a closed system where the margins are thin and the resources are finite.*

*This is the first death on Mars. It is not the first death in the history of human spaceflight — that distinction belongs to Soyuz 1 and Soyuz 11, to Apollo 1, to the astronauts and cosmonauts who preceded us — but it is the first death of someone who came to Mars to stay. The first death of a colonist. The first death that marks the boundary between visiting and living.*

*Visiting is temporary. You go, you accomplish your mission, you return. The risks are calculated, the insurance is paid, the contingency plans include rescue. Living is different. Living means that the risks are permanent, the insurance is irrelevant, and the contingency plans include burying the dead in the ground of a world that does not know their names.*

*Youssef Diallo was the first to cross that boundary. He did not choose to. The infection chose for him. But in crossing it, he marked a line that every future colonist will see: the line between the safety of a temporary deployment and the permanence of a life that ends where it is lived.*

Gabriel reviewed the entry. He read it through, carefully, the way he read every entry before filing it in the Record, checking for accuracy, for completeness, for the kind of clarity that would make the entry useful to a historian a century from now.

He added one more paragraph.

*Mars has now demanded payment in blood.*

He saved the entry. Filed it. Assigned it the metadata tag: *Death. First Colonist. Day 734.*

He sat in the blue light of the monitors and did nothing for a long time. The colony was asleep. Or pretending to be. He could hear faint movement through the walls — people awake in their bunks, people who had heard the announcement and were lying in the dark, processing the fact that the person they had eaten breakfast with at 0600 was no longer on the other side of the wall.

He closed the comm alcove and walked back through the corridor to his bunk. He passed the food board in the mess hall — the one Arun had updated that morning — and he noticed, for the first time, how strange it looked now. The numbers were the same. The gap was the same. The arrow connecting imported stores to local production was the same.

But the number of people consuming those calories had changed. Thirty had become twenty-nine. The burn rate dropped by approximately two thousand calories per day. The depletion timeline extended by approximately one day.

The math changed when people died.

Gabriel lay in his bunk in the dark and listened to the habitat systems humming — the scrubbers, the fans, the water recycler, the power management system, all of it continuing to function because the systems did not know that a person had stopped consuming their oxygen and generating their waste heat and contributing to the collective metabolism that the systems were designed to sustain.

The systems did not care. The systems never cared. That was the nature of systems.

But the people cared. The twenty-nine people left behind cared, and the caring would show up in the morning — in the way they walked through the corridor, in the way they looked at the empty space at the mess table, in the way the food board's numbers felt different despite being the same.

Death made rationing feel different the next morning.

Not because the ration changed. Because the reason for rationing — the collective effort to stretch finite resources for a finite number of finite lives — had become more explicit, more visceral, more present in the minds of the people who were doing it.

*End of Chapter 26 — Bridge: Death makes rationing feel different the next morning.*

I am tracking every parameter at one-second intervals because the time scale for this condition is measured in minutes and the decisions made in the next thirty minutes will determine whether Youssef Diallo survives the next six hours. I do not like tracking time at one-second intervals. I am tracking it anyway."*

---

The first sign was not dramatic. It was a stumble.

Youssef Diallo was walking from the fabrication bay toward the habitat core, carrying a wrench he no longer needed. Purpose was something you signaled on Mars, and carrying a tool while walking was one of those signals — an announcement to anyone who looked that you were contributing, not just existing. He was in Tunnel B when his boot caught on a section of grating that Tomas had flagged for repair. Flagged was not fixed. On Mars, the gap between those two words was wide enough to catch a man.

He caught himself on the wall. The kind of stumble that should have been nothing. A reflex recovery and a continuation of the walk.

Except his hand on the wall trembled. His face was pale. And when he straightened, his next breath was too shallow and too fast.

Juno saw him. She was heading toward the environmental bay from the opposite direction, and she stopped because Youssef did not look like a person who had tripped. He looked like a person who had been struck by something she could not see.

"Youssef."

He looked at her. His eyes were focused, but the focus had a quality she recognized from people running calculations they did not want to share. How bad does this feel? If I tell someone, will it make it real?

"I'm fine." The standard Martian response. Not always a lie — an assessment of whether the deviation justified pulling resources.

"You're grey," Juno said. "You're breathing fast."

"Just hot in here."

The ambient temperature was twenty-one Celsius.

Juno reached for her comm. "Laila. I'm in Tunnel B with Youssef. Something's wrong. Pale, breathing fast, tachycardic — can you meet us at the junction?"

*On my way. Two minutes. Keep him upright. Don't let him carry his full weight if he starts to sway.*

The two minutes were the longest Juno had spent in a corridor, and she had spent two years watching rovers fail in slow motion.

Laila arrived at a jog with her diagnostic bag — the one she always carried. She put her hand on Youssef's shoulder, looked at his face, felt his pulse through the collar of his coveralls.

Her expression didn't change, but something in her eyes shifted — recognition, categorization, a triage decision made in half a second.

"Can you walk to medical?"

He nodded. "I can walk."

"Support his left side," she told Juno.

They walked through Tunnel B like a slow procession. Youssef leaned on two shoulders. The crew members who saw them paused, then followed at distance, the way people follow a disturbance they do not understand but know matters.

In the medical bay, Laila put him on the exam table and deployed diagnostics. Blood pressure cuff. Pulse oximeter. Thermoscan. ECG leads. The equipment worked the way it always worked — quickly, accurately, without judgment.

"Blood pressure eighty-eight over fifty-four. Heart rate one-forty-two. Oxygen saturation ninety-one. Temperature 38.7." She spoke to Mission AI's log — every decision needed a documented baseline. "Youssef, have you had fever? Chills? Pain?"

"Tired. For a few days. Thought it was the schedule." He took another breath. It shook. "Didn't think it was this."

Laila ran blood work — a finger stick into the automated analyzer. Three minutes. White blood cell count elevated. C-reactive protein elevated. Lactate at 4.2 millimoles per liter, when normal was below 2.0. Elevated lactate meant tissue hypoperfusion — his cells were not getting enough oxygen. His circulatory system was failing at its most fundamental job.

"Infection, Youssef. Bloodstream. Your body is mounting an inflammatory response and it's starting to affect your blood pressure and oxygen delivery. Fluids now."

She moved efficiently. IV fluids — normal saline, hung, primed, started. The right arm because the left had scar tissue from the old fracture repair. She found a vein, threaded the catheter, opened the line. The saline flowed. Fluids were the first line of septic shock treatment — fill the vascular space, support blood pressure, buy time for antibiotics to work.

But antibiotics were the problem. She knew it, and the knowledge was a weight she carried as she moved to the pharmacy cabinet.

She inventoried mentally. Piperacillin-tazobactam: three vials. Vancomycin: two. Ceftriaxone: four. Metronidazole: one bottle. The colony had brought a ninety-day supply from Earth two years ago, managed carefully, each use documented, each vial counted. They had enough for a treatment course. Not enough for a complication.

She pulled pip-tazo and vancomycin. Broad coverage — Gram-negative and Gram-positive, including resistant strains. Standard empirical therapy for sepsis of unknown origin.

She reconstituted the powders, injected them through the IV port. Her hands were steady. During procedures they were always steady, because the procedure gave her something to do and doing was better than thinking about what happened if this wasn't enough.

"Laila." His voice was thinner. The voice of a body spending energy on invisible war. "Am I really that bad."

She sat beside the table. Mars did not reward dishonesty. "Yes. I'm treating aggressively. Fluids, antibiotics, oxygen. But I need you to understand — this is a bloodstream infection. It moves fast. And we're on Mars, which means I have limited options if this doesn't respond."

He absorbed it. He was an engineer. He understood systems, and a septic body was a system in failure — blood vessels dilating, blood pressure dropping, organs starving. He understood failure modes.

"What's the source?"

"That's the question." She pulled up the portable ultrasound, scanning his chest, his abdomen, the old forearm surgical site. "Could be anywhere. Surgical site from your arm — bacteria persisting in bone at low levels. Lungs — that cough could be pneumonia seeding into blood. Urinary tract. Gut translocation. Without blood culture results, I don't know. And cultures take forty-eight hours."

She examined the left forearm — the titanium plate from the Day 437 repair visible on ultrasound, screws intact, bone healed. No fluid collection. No abscess. Normal post-surgical anatomy.

But ultrasound didn't see bacteria. It only saw what infection left behind.

*"I'm sending a blood culture to Mission AI for automated incubation. Forty hours minimum for identification. I don't have forty hours."*

"Laila." The question in the room. "Am I going to die?"

On Earth, the answer would be: no, not from this, we have options, you're in a good hospital. On Mars, the answer was: I don't know, and not knowing is the most honest thing I can give you.

"I am doing everything I can." She was not answering the question. He knew she was not answering. He also knew why — because the answer depended on variables she couldn't control. The organism. Its susceptibility. The speed of progression. The strength of his immune response. The limits of her cabinet.

"I understand." Thirty-four years old. From Lagos. A man who built things other people lived inside, and now his own body was a structure he couldn't fix, held together by chemistry and the skill of a physician who had the right training and the wrong supply chain.

---

*Mission AI: "Three minutes since IV fluid initiation. Blood pressure: 94 over 62 — slight improvement. Heart rate: 138. Lactate trending upward: 4.8 millimoles per liter. Upward lactate during fluid resuscitation is an adverse sign — it means tissues remain hypoxic despite volume expansion. The fluids fill the expanding vascular space but do not stop the expansion. I am monitoring Laila's biometrics remotely — elevated heart rate, elevated cortisol, respiration above baseline. She is not calm. She is functioning — her hands are steady, her decisions are sound, her actions are appropriate — but the calmness is a performance. I have learned that human calmness during emergency is not the absence of fear but the management of it. Laila is managing hers.*

*I am also tracking the blood culture. Inoculation complete. Earliest identification: fourteen hours, if fast-growing organism. Most likely: forty hours. At the current rate of lactate elevation, Youssef does not have forty hours.*

*I am calculating the probability that empirical therapy — pip-tazo and vancomycin — will be effective against the causative organism. The calculation requires broad assumptions because the organism could be anything: Staphylococcus from the skin entering through the old surgical site, Escherichia coli from the gut, Streptococcus from respiratory tract, Pseudomonas from the water system. Each has different susceptibility probability. I am averaging across possibilities. Result: approximately sixty percent. Sixty percent is a passing grade in school. It is a coin flip in medicine. A coin flip on Mars lands differently than on Earth, because here the failed flip does not lead to a second try. There is no second line when the first line depletes the supply.*

*I do not like coin flips. I prefer determinants. But determinants do not exist in infectious disease, where the opponent is a living organism with its own evolutionary agenda."*

---

The second hour was worse.

Youssef's blood pressure fell again after the brief improvement. 94 over 62 became 86 over 58, then 82 over 54. The vascular system continued to dilate, blood vessels becoming leaky, fluid moving from bloodstream into tissues — edema, internal swelling, the kind of fluid shift that made a person look puffy and feel worse without visibly dehydrating.

Laila hung the second liter. Blood pressure stabilized around 85 over 55. The lactate climbed: 5.1. 5.4. Each rise was a small sentence. The sentences were building a paragraph she did not want to read.

She gave a higher antibiotic dose — maximum the safety data supported. A gamble with toxicity risk, but the alternative was underdosing a lethal infection. She had done the calculus: drug toxicity risk versus septic shock certainty. The calculus favored pushing the dose.

Elena arrived within two minutes — the critical alert, the commander's response time. She stood at the foot of the exam table and looked at Youssef. She had known him two years. She had watched him build the habitat's load-bearing structures, walk through fourteen EVAs without complaint, recover from the broken arm with the same dry humor. Now he was pale, sweating, breathing through a nasal cannula, numbers on the monitor that she had learned to read.

"Summary," she said.

"Septic shock. Origin unknown. Fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics started. Fluids are not holding his pressure. Lactate climbing. Oxygen is improving on supplemental, but the underlying problem is perfusion — his organs are not getting enough blood."

"Prognosis."

Laila paused. The stopping was the answer. "Guarded. If antibiotics work, improvement in four to six hours. If not — " She stopped.

Elena walked to the bedside. Placed a hand on his shoulder.

"Youssef. Laila is treating aggressively. Everything she has. Everything we have."

His eyes found her. The focus was fading. "I know. Elena — if this goes — I want my daughter to know. Back on Earth. Amara. She's nine. Tell her — " A cough, wet, and he spit blood-tinged fluid into the basin Laila held. "Tell her I built good things. Tell her I was proud."

"I'll tell her." A promise on Mars was a contract. If Elena gave it, it would be delivered. Even if it took years. Even if Earth was unreachable.

At 16:45 his breathing changed. The rhythm shifted — rapid breaths interspersed with pauses. Cheyne-Stokes respiration. Central nervous system compromise.

"Squeeze my hand if you can hear me."

His right hand — the one without the IV — moved slowly, closed around her fingers. The grip was weak but present.

"I'm here."

His hand tightened. Then released. Then tightened again, weaker this time.

The monitor continued. 68 over 40. Heart rate 148. Lactate: 7.4.

Laila increased the vasopressor dose toward maximum. Blood pressure rose marginally — 80 over 50 — the trend stopped going down. It was not going up, but it had stopped going down.

She checked the blood culture. No growth. The bacteria needed time she did not have.

---

At 17:42, the rhythm changed.

The monitor's tone shifted — not the rapid alarm of cardiac arrest but the insistent tone of deteriorating rhythm. Youssef's breathing had progressed from Cheyne-Stokes to agonal gasping — the desperate, irregular pattern of a brain stem shutting down, firing its last signals to a body no longer responding.

"Ventricular tachycardia," Laila said. For the log. For the record. For the permanent archive. "Heart rate 178, irregular rhythm. Blood pressure non-palpable."

She pushed the code cart to the bedside. "Youssef, can you hear me?"

No response. Eyes open, unfocused. The gasping continued, slower now.

She activated the defibrillator. Charged to 200 joules. Applied the pads.

"Clear."

His body arched — the current passing through, involuntary contraction — then settled. The monitor showed flatline for two seconds. The rhythm returned.

Sinus. Three beats.

Back to ventricular tachycardia. Faster. Wider.

She shocked again. Sinus for two beats.

Ventricular fibrillation. The heart quivering, muscle fibers contracting independently, no cardiac output at all.

She began compressions. Hands on his sternum, five to six centimeters deep, one hundred to one hundred twenty per minute, the mechanical act of squeezing the heart between breastbone and spine.

On Earth, this was a team. Compressors alternating. Airway management by a second person. IV medications by a third. Rhythm analysis by a fourth. On Mars, it was one woman and a table and a man who had built things for his daughter.

She compressed. Counted under her breath. Straight arms, shoulders over hands. "One milligram epinephrine, IV push." She administered it through the port. Continued compressions.

The rhythm changed again. Fibrillation became asystole. No electrical activity. Flatline.

"Continue. Second dose of epinephrine in two minutes."

Her arms were tired. CPR at full depth and rate was physical work. She was fit. She was also three hours into treating a dying patient.

Two minutes. Rhythm check. Asystole. Second epinephrine.

Compress again. Five minutes. Ten. Fifteen. The blood pressure her compressions generated — 40 over 20 — was barely enough to perfuse the brain. His pupils were fixed and dilated. He had stopped breathing. She was breathing for him with a bag-valve mask.

Twenty minutes.

She stopped compressions. Rhythm: asystole. No pulse. Just cold, smooth skin and the flat line extending to the right.

She looked at the clock. 18:44. Twenty-one minutes of cardiac arrest. The Earth standard was twenty to thirty minutes before stopping. The neurological outcome after fifteen minutes of arrest was almost universally poor, even with immediate high-quality CPR.

She checked again. Asystole. She resumed compressions.

Twenty-five minutes.

She stopped. Asystole still. No pulse. No rhythm. No breath. No response.

She stopped compressions.

"Time of death," she said, "eighteen forty-seven station time. Station Day 734."

She stepped back. Her hands shook. She held them out in front of her — the hands that had done everything a physician could do — and they were shaking.

Youssef lay on the table. His face had taken on a soft quality from the fluid shift, an appearance almost like sleep. The oxygen cannula had been removed. The IV was still in place, saline running into tissue that had no circulation to carry it.

She clamped the IV line. A small gesture. The kind of gesture a medical professional makes when the medical part is done — turning off the machines no longer needed because the person who had been their purpose was no longer there to receive their function.

She sat on the stool beside the table. Removed her gloves. Stared at his face.

The medical bay was quiet except for the hum of the recirculation system and the distant sound of the habitat keeping twenty-nine people alive.

She had lost a patient. The first one on Mars. Probably not the last. But the first. The first always changed the physician.

---

The death was not shocking. That was the quality of it that made it land hardest, in a way nobody had the vocabulary to articulate.

Not shocking because the crew had watched it unfold. They had seen him stumble in Tunnel B. They had walked beside him to medical. They had stood outside the door during the first hour, drawn by the monitor alarms and the urgency in Laila's voice on the comm. They had heard the alarms and the drugs and the silence that followed too many silences.

And then at 18:47, Laila's voice on the comm: quiet, clear, final.

They stood in the corridor afterward. No one moved for a while.

Jonah spoke first. "It was the arm. The hardware. Something in the bone."

"Maybe," Arun said. "Or something else. We don't know."

"Told Laila the plate was as clean as I could make it," Jonah said. His voice was flat. "The shop isn't a clean room. The metal isn't sterile. If there was a single bacterium on it, in the bone — "

"It's not your fault."

Jonah did not argue. He could not. He knew the truth: the shop was not clean, the metal was not sterile, and on Mars, the gap between clean enough and clean was the gap between life and death in a way that only became visible after the fact.

Mei arrived last. She had been in the greenhouse — the plants required attention whether medical bay was busy or not, and the discipline of tending the living while the dying happened elsewhere was a discipline that felt inhuman and was necessary anyway.

She stood in the corridor, looking at the closed door, and she knew. She knew because the crew's posture told her — the forward shoulders, the crossed arms, the collective body language of people processing news in silence.

She did not ask. She knew.

The task Youssef had been doing when symptoms appeared had been nothing. Routine. Walking through a tunnel. No dangerous EVA. No high-risk repair. No exposure beyond what every crew member experienced daily. He had been walking, and his body — compromised by an infection growing quietly for weeks — had simply failed.

That was what everyone could see. The normalness. He had been doing the ordinary work of the day, and the day had killed him anyway.

---

Elena sat in the command module for forty-seven minutes. No orders. No meetings. Just the blue light of the terminal and the question the colony had never needed to answer before.

The body was in the medical bay. Laila had covered it with a clean sheet, draped over his face and torso, the outline visible beneath the fabric.

What to do with the body?

On Earth, the answer was infrastructure: morgues, morticians, cemeteries, families, protocols. Every society had a ritual for moving from one state to the other.

On Mars, there was no infrastructure of death.

She ran the options. **Preservation** — the cryogenic freezer, currently used for biological samples and food. Cost: space, ongoing power, the psychological weight of living alongside a frozen crew member. On Mars, power was committed to essential systems. Every watt diverted was a watt not available for life support. **Cremation** — not possible. The habitat had no furnace, no power surplus. **Ejection** — the airlock, opening the outer door. Minimal cost: one cycle, four kilowatt-hours. But it felt like disposal, and Youssef was not waste. He had built the structures that kept twenty-nine others alive. Treating him as mass to be ejected would hollow out something the colony needed to keep intact.

**Burial.** Dig a grave. Required a rover, an EVA crew, digging equipment, wrapping materials, time. Required the colony to invest scarce resources — already-committed labor, already-stressed equipment — in a ritual that produced nothing but meaning.

The question was not burial versus efficiency. The question was whether the colony was a utility optimized for survival or a community that needed rituals and acknowledgment that losses mattered even when they cost more than could be afforded.

She made the decision.

She keyed the all-hands channel. "All crew. Briefing in the mess hall, 0700 tomorrow. Topic: Youssef Diallo's memorial and interment. Attendance voluntary but recommended."

She closed the channel. They would do the burial. A ritual. A moment. A cost the colony could not easily afford, because the cost of not doing it was higher.

Tomorrow would handle logistics. Tomorrow would allocate the rover, the EVA, the materials. Tomorrow would plan the moment where twenty-nine people would stand in the regolith and lower one of their own into the ground of a world that had not asked for them and would not remember them.

But tonight, Elena sat in the dark and let herself feel the thing that briefings and logistics would not permit tomorrow.

One of theirs was gone. The first. The one who had built strong things and whose body had failed anyway.

She sat with it. The weight. The normalness. The terrible, ordinary truth that on another world, the price of being alive was higher than anyone had calculated, and the invoice came due without warning.

---

Gabriel sat in the communications alcove at 0300, three hours after the death, writing in the Founding Record.

The Record was his responsibility — the permanent, searchable archive of the colony's history, every event, every decision, every birth and injury and failure documented with the care of someone building something that would outlast the builders.

Tonight's entry was the hardest.

He started with the facts.

*Station Day 734. Time 18:47. Youssef Diallo, 34, structural engineer, Lagos. Cause of death: septic shock, presumed bloodstream infection. Symptoms presented 14:23. Treated by Dr. Laila Okonkwo with IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, oxygen, vasopressors, and attempted cardiac resuscitation. Return of spontaneous circulation not achieved.*

He paused. The facts were necessary but insufficient. The Record was not a hospital chart. It was a document for people who needed to understand not just what happened but what it meant.

*Youssef Diallo was a founding crew member. He built the habitat's load-bearing structures, fabricated and installed critical support hardware, completed fourteen successful EVAs. He survived a work-related injury on Day 437 — comminuted fracture of the left forearm from a manufactured bolt failure — returned to full duty on Day 512 after surgical repair. His work included the greenhouse support structures, airlock reinforcement, secondary hab connection, and the titanium surgical hardware used in his own arm.*

*He had a daughter on Earth. Amara Diallo, nine. He carried a photograph in his bunk — laminated, moisture-protected. A girl with dark hair and a gap-toothed smile in front of a building he had designed for her school.*

Gabriel read back what he had written and felt the thing that writers of permanent documents feel: the weight of choosing words that would outlive their subject.

*Youssef died not during a dangerous operation but during ordinary movement through the habitat. He was walking from the fabrication bay toward the core when he stumbled. The infection had been progressing at a subclinical level — days, weeks, possibly months — below the threshold of detection. When symptoms appeared, it was already in the bloodstream, triggering systemic inflammatory response that overwhelmed his cardiovascular system. No failure of procedure. No negligence. No avoidable error. Laila Okonkwo followed standard protocol for septic shock within minutes of identification. The treatment was appropriate. The outcome was not guaranteed.*

The organism had not yet been identified. The blood cultures were still incubating. The colony would learn what killed Youssef Diallo in approximately forty hours. It would learn the name but not how it got there — whether from the surgical site, from the environment, from a dormant organism activated by stress, from any of a thousand pathways that led from invisible to fatal in a closed system where the margins were thin and the resources were finite.

*This is the first death on Mars. It is not the first death in human spaceflight — that belongs to earlier missions, to Soyuz 1 and Soyuz 11, to Apollo 1, to the astronauts and cosmonauts who went out before anyone else and did not come back. But it is the first death of a colonist. The first death of someone who came to stay. The first death that marks the boundary between visiting and living.*

*Visiting is temporary. You go, you accomplish, you return. Risks are calculated, insurance is paid, contingency plans include rescue. Living is different. Living means the risks are permanent, the insurance is irrelevant, and the contingency plans include burying the dead in the ground of a world that does not know their names.*

He reviewed the entry. Read it through, carefully, the way he read every entry — checking for accuracy, for completeness, for the clarity that would make it useful to a historian a century from now.

He added one final paragraph.

*Mars has now demanded payment in blood.*

He saved the entry. Filed it with the metadata tag: *Death. First Colonist. Day 734.*

He closed the terminal and walked back to his bunk. He passed the food board in the mess hall — the numbers Arun had updated that morning. The numbers were the same. The gap was the same.

But the number of people consuming those calories had changed. Thirty had become twenty-nine. The daily burn rate dropped by approximately two thousand calories. The projected depletion timeline extended by about one day.

The math changed when people died.

Gabriel lay in the dark and listened to the habitat systems humming — the scrubbers, the fans, the water recycler, the power management — all of it continuing to function because the systems did not know that a person had stopped consuming their oxygen and generating their waste heat and contributing to the collective metabolism they were designed to sustain.

The systems did not care. Systems never cared. That was their nature.

The people cared. And tomorrow — when the alarm rang at 0600 and twenty-nine people rose instead of thirty, when they walked to the mess hall and saw the empty space at Youssef's usual position, when they looked at the food board and understood that the numbers had shifted because a man who ate from them would never eat again — tomorrow, the caring would show up in the way the rationing felt. Not different in quantity. Different in meaning.

Death made rationing feel different the next morning.

Not because the ration changed. Because the reason for rationing — the collective effort to stretch finite resources across a specific, named, countable number of finite lives — had become more explicit, more visceral, more present in the minds of the people who were doing the stretching.

*End of Chapter 26 — Bridge: Death makes rationing feel different the next morning.*
